Mr. ROBERT FORKE (Brandon) moved that the House go into committee on Bill No. 47, to incorporate The United Church of Canada.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 2-Date of coming into force subject to decision in pending action and reference to Supreme Court.

Mr. Chairman, it is my desire to move in connection with this clause an amendment which will have for its purpose the striking out of the clause and the substitution of another.
This is one of the most important bills that have ever been before the parliament of Canada; and for this reason, that perhaps a greater number of people in the Dominion of Canada are interested in this bill than have ever been interested in any other-certainly any other private bill-that has been before the House. This bill has for its purpose the consummation of the union that was agreed upon by three negotiating bodies of Christians, known as the Presbyterian Church in Canada, the Methodist Church of Canada, and the Congregational Churches of Canada. This bill passed through the Private Bills committee, and in the course of its progress through that committee certain amendments were made to it which alter the bill very materially, and which are considered by the promoters to change in very large measure its effect.
Before entering upon a discussion of these amendments which now appear in the reprinted copy of the bill-a slight change in the preamble, together with the amended clause which now appears as clause 2-let me indicate what I think should be the guiding principles of this committee in approaching the subject, and what the attitude of parliament should be in connection with this bill. It is not the function of parliament to decide upon questions of doctrine or church polity. Unfortunately, during the discussion before the Privat; Bills committee, perhaps because there was some little mistake in the wording of the original bill, and because some of those opposing the bill introduced these matters in connection with their opposition, the discussion for a time did centre around questions of doctrine. In my judgment, these things should never have been considered at all. While there was a little misunderstanding in regard to the bill as first
drafted, it is now made quite clear that in the request that the basis of union be ratified as such, there is no thought that parliament should ratify this or any other form of doctrine or belief. Nowhere in the British Empire, neither in the Motherland nor in any of the great self-governing dominions, will it be seriously contended that the civil power has any right to dictate to men the religious beliefs they shall hold or the manner in which they shall give expression to their thoughts and aspirations in things spiritual.
I have been frequently asked why it is necessary to get power from parliament in order to consummate church unioq. The fact that such a question should be asked indicates the deep-rooted conviction that matters of faith and worship lie outside the jurisdiction of the civil power, and woe to that government or parliament that shall attempt to lay unholy hands on the Ark of the Covenant. What then is the purpose of this measure? It is not to define our creeds. Is it, then, to define our polity, the manner in which the church shall carry on its affairs? No. It simply asks that Methodists, Congregationalism and Presbyterians shall be given legal sanction to administer their affairs according to the terms that have been mutually agreed upon. In coming to a decision as to whether this sanction should be given, members of parliament, as such, have a right, in my judgment, to ask only two questions. Members of parliament should approach this question as members of parliament. We are here, not as individual members of any of the negotiating churches, not to give expression to our individual views; we had that opportunity when the matter was before our various churches. We are here now as members of parliament to decide whether this legal sanction shall be given; and I say that in my judgment we should ask two questions, and two only: First, has each one of the contracting parties, in the various steps that have been taken in arriving at the conclusion that organic union with the other two as desirable, followed the course that best harmonizes with its constitution and accepted method of procedure? Second, does this bill make a proper provision for the rights of minorities who may not desire to enter into the union?
I shall not discuss that second question at this time, because that will come up as we discuss the various clauses of the bill, but I would just like to make this general assertion at this time:	That never before in the history of the various unions that have taken place has such generous provision been made

United Church of Canada
for tlie rights of minorities. Having satisfied ourselves that the correct procedure has in all cases been followed and that minority rights have been properly protected, parliament in my judgment has nothing else to do but to pass this legislation. To do otherwise would be to arrogate to itself functions it does not possess.
In considering the question of the procedure that has been followed it must be borne in miind that it is not necessary that all the churches should have followed the same lines. Congregational procedure would, of necessity, differ from Methodist procedure, and Presbyterian procedure would differ from both. Perhaps I might indicate briefly just what these differences in procedure are. Under Congregational polity, which recognizes each local church as a self-contained and self-governing unit, the only way by which these units could enter into a union was by each local church voting itself in. That was recognized from the very beginning. There was no central body made up of delegates or representatives of these local bodies that had any authority except to carry out the instructions given by the local churches. It is true that the Congregational Union of Canada on more than one occasion voted for union with the Methodists and Presbyterians, but that carried no authority; it was simply an expression of opinion by the delegates from .the local churches that this union was desirable. I mention this matter because it has an important bearing on the question whether the proper procedure was observed by the other negotiating churches. The 'Methodist chinch is a well organized body under representative government. The authority derived in the first place from the people and vested in various church courts known as quarterly boards, district meetings, conferences and the General Conference. Thus when the General Conference of the Methodist church votes in favour of union it is representing a decision that has been arrived at progressively through the lower courts of the church. Under the Methodist system it is inconceivable that any local Methodist circuit should have power to vote itself out of the union, except as a matter of grace after union had been accomplished. To take any other course would be to do violence to what has always been the genius of the Methodist system.
The procedure provided by the Presbyterian church is similar to that of the Methodist church, except that in the case of the Presbyterian church there is an additional safeguard against hasty action provided by the Barrier Act. Under the operation of this act a decision

arrived at by the assembly does not become binding upon the church until the matter has been again passed upon by the presbyteries. It must be clearly kept in mind that in the Presbyterian system there is no provision for a plebiscite of the membership before submission to the church courts, or for a referendum after the matter has been passed upon by these courts. True, a vote of the members and adherents was taken, but this had no constitutional effect, and was solely for the purpose of enabling the presbyteries to arrive at a decision as to whether or not union was desirable.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to enter into a discussion as to the relative merits of these different methods of procedure. It would be expected that, as a Congrega-tionalist, I would be in favour of the congregational system. But that is neither here nor there. I would have no right at this time, and I think the House would have no right, to dictate to any church the method by which it shall arrive at its decision. My only concern, and I think the only concern of this House, should be as to whether each one of the negotiating bodies followed its own method of procedure.
Let me now proceed to answer the question: Has each church observed the proper procedure in arriving at its decision? There can be no question as regards the Congregational church. It is true, there are individual churches, one or two, that have not voted to come into the union; but the great majority of the united membership have voted in favour, as also the great majority of the individual churches. There can be no question then but that the procedure is in harmony with the Congregational system; neither can there be any question as to the procedure followed by the Methodist church; and neither in the case of the Congregational nor of the Methodist church is there any organized opposition to the consummation of the union I hrough the bill that is now before parliament. But it is different in the case of the Presbyterian church. From the very beginning of this movement looking towards church union there has been in that church a very considerable element that has been opposed to such steps being taken, and this element is to-day offering opposition to the passage of the bill.
Now, as I am not, and never have been a member of the Presbyterian church I did not, during the progress of the church union negotiations through the various courts, pay very much attention to the matter except in a

United Church oj Canada
general way. Recognizing however, that I would have duties to perform as a member of this House I felt it incumbent upon me to put myself in a position to answer to my own satisfaction the two questions alone that seem to me to be vital:	Has the proper procedure been observed? Have the rights of minorities been protected? By personal conversation and by reading union and anti-union literature I have satisfied myself that the course followed by the. Presbyterian church has been in harmony with its own constitution, and that the proposed bill makes all reasonable provision for the protection of minorities' rights. I shall therefore not attempt to recite ir. detail the various steps taken by the courts of the Presbyterian church by which they reached their final decision. These steps were not taken hastily. They were taken after the utmost deliberation covering a long period of years; and there is no question n my mind that the action taken by the church leaders in carrying out the decisions arrived at through the various church courts meets with the requirements of the Presbyterian constitution and the wishes of the great majority of the members and the adherents of the church. Knowing little of the Presbyterian system, except in a general way, I entered upon the study of this subject with a good deal of interest, and I may say that I gained an increasing admiration for the Presbyterian system when I noticed the calmness and deliberation with which they dealt with the question. Every step was taken in an orderly manner:	First from the lower
courts up to the assembly, then back again to the presbyteries; and in all the steps they took, those steps, it seemed to me. were charalcterized by the utmost deliberation; and I can come to no other conclusion than that the bill is in perfect harmony with the procedure provided by their own church. It is somewhat significant, that little if any objection has been offered to the procedure. It is true that objection was taken to the thing itself. It has been urged that the Presbyterian Assembly had no power to do the thing it did; that to do what it did really meant the destruction of the churlch. I do not think that assertion can be considered as well founded. There is no thought of destruction of any one body, when it unites with another. It never was felt that a branch of the Presbyterian church was destroyed when the union of 1875 took place, neither was it felt that any branch of the Methodist church was destroyed when the union took place in the early eighties. If it is a fact- and it would seem to be a faict-that there
is more difference in faith within the bounds of any one of these churches than there is between any two, it would seem that there is no reason to hold that the identity of any one of the negotiating churches would be sacrificed, any more than was the identity of those churches that entered into the former unions.
Now I come to the amendments that were made to the bill. One amendment proposes that instead of bringing this bill into force by the sanction of this parliament certain matters shall be referred to the civil courts. This would seem to be a direlct challenge to the right of each church to determine its own doctrine, its own polity and its own destiny. When such a challenge as that is issued it seems to me it behooves not only one church but all churches to assert the right of the church to determine for itself through its courts what its destiny shall be Much has been said of the House of Lords' decision in the case of the Scottish church,
. rendered in 1904. It will be remembered that decision was rendered by those who lived in an atmosphere entirely different from that which prevails here. The conception of the relationship of church and state that prevailed in the Old Land until this decision was rendered was entirely different from that which has prevailed among us, and we may safely say that such a decision never could have been accepted in Canada as final. Canadian sentiment in this respect is much more closely in harmony with the sentiment that has prevailed in the United States. I had thought at one time to read a number of extracts from various judgments rendered by United States judges in regard to the relations of church and state which seemed to very clearly harmonize with our own. I shall not however, take time to do that this afternoon, but would only assert that the decision rendered by the House of Lords in 1904 was abhorrent to our conception of the relations of church and state. The situation which arose at that- time was corrected, and the conception of the relation of church and state which now prevails in Britain is represented by the declaratory articles passed by the church and ratified by the Imperial parliament by the act of 1921.
Why do we object to these amendments that were addted to the bill? It should be remembered that the negotiating bodies, from the time that they began their negotiations, had very clearly before their minds that the union would be consummated only by an act of the Imperial parliament and concurrent legislation on the part of the provincial par-

liaments. That was recognized, and during the whole Bourse of the negotiations the thought was to avoid the difficulty that arose in the case of the Scottish church which is very clearly set forth in the appendix to the law on the basis of union. I shall just read one clause making clear that the United church shall have the powers of legislation mentioned in sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 24 of the polity section of the basis of union, subject to the safeguards thereby imposed, in such full and ample manner as to render impossible the existence in connection with the United church of the conditions which have arisen in Scotland in connection with the United Free Church of Scotland, under the decision of the House of Lords, touching its property and doctrine.
The purpose of those who entered into the negotiations leading up to this bill was to avoid litigation, and now the Private Bills committee of this House has forced upon them, or would force upon them, the very thing they sought to avoid. W >
may, I think,, learn from the bill to whicc I have referred, the Imperial act of 1921, affirming the declaratory articles of the Scottish church what ought to be our proper course at this time. This act is very brief, and I think it would be well that not only the act itself, but the declaratory articles as well should be inscribed on the pages of Hansard. I am going to read the act-since it only contains four clauses-and briefly summarize the declaratory articles. In my judgment it throws a great deal of light upon our present situation. This is an act to declare the lawfulness of certain articles declaratory of the constitution of the Church of Scotland in matters spiritual, prepared with the authority of the General Assembly of the church. The preamble reads:
Whereas certain articles declaratory of the constitution of the Church of Scotland in matters spiritual have been prepared with the authority of the General Assembly of the church with a view to facilitate the union of other churches with the Church of Scotland, which articles are set out in the schedule to this act, and together with any modifications of the said articles or additions thereto made in accordance therewith are hereinafter in this act referred to as "the declaratory articles".
And whereas it is expedient that any doubts as to the lawfulness of the declaratory articles should be removed:
Be it therefore enacted by the King's most Excellent Majesty by and with the advice of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and .by the authority of the same, as follows:
1.	The declaratory articles are lawful articles, and the constitution of the Church of Scotland in matters spiritual is as therein set forth and no limitation of the liberty, rights and powers in matters spiritual therein set forth shall be derived in any statute or law affect-

ing the Church of Scotland in matters spiritual at present in force, it being hereby declared that in all questions of construction the declaratory articles shall prevail, and that all such statutes and laws shall be construed in conformity therewith and in subordination thereto, and all such statutes and laws in so far as they are inconsistent with the declaratory articles are hereby repealed and declared to be of no effect.
2.	Nothing contained in this act or in any other act affecting the Church of Scotland shall prejudice the recognition of any other church in Scotland as a Christian church protected by law in the exercise of its spiritual functions.
3.	Subject to the recognition of the matters dealt with in the declaratory articles, as matters spiritual, nothing in this act contained shall affect or prejudice the jurisdiction of the civil courts in relation to any matter of a civil nature.
4.	This act may be cited as the Church of Scotland Act, 1921, and shall come into operation on such date as His Majesty may fix by order in council after the declaratory articles shall have been adopted by an act of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland with the consent of the majority of the presbyteries of the church.
Now the declaratory articles themselves are contained in the schedule. I shall briefly refer to them, although I think it would be as well for the information of the country if the whole of them were inscribed on Hansard.
Section 1 declares the Church of Scotland to be part of the Holy Catholic Church that it adheres to Scottish reformation, that its supreme standard of faith is found in the Old and New Testaments.
Section 2 declares that the Westminster Confession is a subordinate standard, and that it approves of the doctrinal statement therein contained, and the prescription of government therein described.
Section 3 asserts the historical continuity of the Church of Scotland and declares that the continuity of the Church of Scotland and its identity are not prejudiced by the adoption of these articles.
Section 4 deals with the office bearers and mode of election and their authority, and it concludes with these words:
Or give to the civil authority any right of interference with procedure cr the judgment of the church within the sphere of its own government and jurisdiction.
Section 5 asserts the inherent right of the church to interpret and to frame its own statement of faith, to interpret and adopt its own subordinate standards, and to modify these always in relation to the condition of faith set forth in section 1.
Section 6 is simply a general recognition of the church and state, each having its own jurisdiction.
I will read section 7 in full, because it has some important bearing upon this case:
The Church of Scotland believing it to be the will of Christ that His disciples should be all one in the Father and in Him, that the world may believe that the

United Church oj Canada
Father has sent Him, recognizes the obligation to seek and promote union with other churches in which it finds the Word to be purely preached, the sacraments administered according to Christ's ordinance, and discipline rightly exercised; and it has the right to unite with any such church without loss of its identity on terms which this church finds to be consistent with these articles.
That is left for the church itself to determine.
Section 8 reads:
The church has the right to interpret these articles, and, subject to the safeguards for deliberate action and legislation provided by the church itself, to modify or add to them; but always consistently with the provisions of the first article hereof, adherence to which, as interpreted by the church, is essential to its continuity and corporate life. Any proposal for a modification of or addition to these articles which may be approved of by the General Assembly, shall, before it can be enacted by the assembly, be transmitted by way of overture to presbyteries in at least two immediately successive years. If the overture shall receive the approval, with or without suggested amendment, of two-thirds of the whole of the presbyteries of the church, the assembly may revise the overture in the light of any suggestions by presbyteries, and may transmit the overture when so revised to presbyteries for their consent. If the overture as transmitted in its final form shall receive the consent of not less than two-thirds- of the whole of the presbyteries of the church, the General Assembly may, if it deems it expedient, modify or add to these articles in terms of the said overture. But if the overture as transmitted in its final form shall not receive the requisite consent, the same or a similar proposal shall not be again transmitted for the consent of presbyteries until an interval of five years after the failure to obtain the requisite consent has been reported to the General Assembly.
Section 9 reads as follows:
Subject to the provisions of the foregoing articles and the powers of amendment therein contained, the constitution of the Church of Scotland in matters spiritual is hereby anew ratified and confirmed by the church.
Now turn back to the second part of the preamble which says:
Whereas it is expedient that any doubts as to the lawfulness of the declaratory articles should be removed :
That is, in order to set at rest any doubts as to the lawfulness of these articles, the Imperial parliament passed this statute.
That is very similar to the situation which confronts us. These negotiating churches came together. They recognized there might possibly be some doubt and they came to parliament asking parliament to pass an act in order that the doubt might be removed and that it might be settled for all time. The Private Bills committee, in its wisdom, or otherwise, said, "You have asked for legislation, but we will give you litigation; go to the courts". Instead of this parliament doing what the British parliament did, setting all these matters at rest as regards the Church
of Scotland and any other churches in Scotland, this parliament is asked to take an entirely different course. But we say, no; we object to being forced into the courts when our purpose from the beginning wgs to avoid litigation.
I will just briefly indicate one or two other reasons why this clause should be deleted from the bill. The churches have now been twenty years in a period of negotiations. The work of the churches has been carried on not perhaps in the orderly and systematic manner in which it was carried on previously. Temporary arrangements have been made. It is not desirable that this condition should any longer continue. Not only is it true in the West, but it is also true in eastern Canada in many districts, that until this legislation is passed the churches cannot carry on their work with the system, the orderliness, the force, that they otherwise could have done. Therefore, it is not wise that we should ask them to accept, or that we should force upon them, the delay that would necessarily be incurred if this clause were allowed to remain in the bill. Because it is by no means certain how long it would take to reach anything like a decision. "The law's delays" we know are proverbial, and we have no right to force any longer delay upon these churches.
And does any one imagine for a moment that even if an adverse decision should be given in the courts that that would finally settle the matter? I cannot imagine for a moment that the Presbyterian church or any other church would be satisfied with a decision of the civil courts that would impugn the rights of its own courts to decide its own doctrine, polity and destiny. If doubt should be thrown upon the authority of its General Assembly, the Presbyterian church would come back to this parliament, just as the Church of Scotland went to the British parliament, and would ask, and would have a right to receive from this parliament, legislation confirming it in the exercise of its rights as a church. Therefore, we cannot think that the matter would be settled even if an adverse decision should be given. Parliament has the authority to settle the matter right now, so why should that not be done?
Other reasons might be urged. It might be worth while pointing to the recent vote of the General Assembly at Owen Sound. It has been contended that the General Assembly has not represented the Presbyterian church; but for the benefit of those who are not familiar with church procedure, it might be indicated that the personnel of one General Assembly is never the same as that of the one that preceded it. I am not certain of the number, but
United Church of Canada

four or five times the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church has pronounced on this question in one phase or another and always by large majorities, the last vote taken at Owen Sound showing the largest majority of all. The General Assembly represents only one-sixth of the ministers and an equal number of the elders. These are chosen in turn, so that you have not the votes of a body of men meeting together year after year, but the votes of a body that differs absolutely in its personnel every year. Surely that is a reason for holding that the General Assembly does represent the will of the Presbyterian church.
One matter which has not been referred to during the course of the debate, but to which I would wish to refer just at this point, is that this question has been discussed almost altogether from the standpoint of the Presbyterian church and the opposing element in that church; but it should be remembered that there are three negotiating bodies, not only the Presbyterian church, but the Methodist church and the Congregational church. Hitherto, those representing the other churches have stood aside. But they have some rights now that should be recognised by this parliament, and delay should no longer be forced upon the Methodist church or the Congregational church. I do not think this parliament would be wise in ignoring those rights. While we have not asserted them very strongly up to this point, I think that at this time it is fitting that it should be made very clear that this is not simply a matter in regard to which the dissenting minority of the Presbyterian church are interested; but it is a matter in which a very large proportion of the Presbyterian church are interested as well as these other two negotiating bodies; and, speaking for the other negotiating bodies, we are satisfied that no civil court will declare the inadequacy of the Presbyterian courts. We are satisfied that the legislation that we are asking for is good legislation and will hold, and we are asking this parliament to give us this legislation.
There is no question of the right of parliament in this matter. Parliament may pass this legislation' or it may refuse it. But I want to point out that there is absolutely no precedent for refusing legislation when bodies of Christians, desiring to have their union consummated, come before parliament or any legislature. The request has always been granted as a matter of course. When churches through their own action or by the means provided by their own constitution, have determined to enter a union, parliament has always ratified those unions. So, we say: You

have power to pass this legislation; you have power to refuse it; but do not send us to the courts to meet litigation which is exactly what we have been trying all these years to avoid. Therefore, I beg to move the following amendment:
That the whole of section 2 of the said bill be stricken out and the following substituted therefor:
2. This act shall come into force on the 10th day of June, 1925, except the provisions required to permit the vote provided for in section 10 being taken, which shall come into force on the 10th day of December, 1924.

I
should like to deal for a few moments, not only with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), but with the history of the negotiations which have led up to the introduction of this bill, that is the first bill as introduced into parliament and considered by the Private Bills committee, with the bill as amended and reported to parliament by the chairman c f the select standing committee on Private Bills and also with the amendments which have been moved thereto by the hon. member for Lisgar. In order to understand this question properly, we have to go back a good many years. The hon. member for Lisgar told us in a few words some of the things which happened in regard to this great question. But before this parliament can give an intelligent vote on this question, we must look at the question from every angle. What are the facts with regard to the negotiations as mentioned by the hon. member for Lisgar? In the year 1904, the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada and the Methodist Conference met in the same city, and three members of the Presbyterian Assembly were instructed by that assembly to go over to the church where the Methodist Conference was meeting and extend to them the felicitations of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada. During the course of the remarks made by these three gentlemen, the last speaker, Principal Patrick, without any instructions from the Presbyterian General Assembly, in his remarks held out the hope that the union between those two great churches might be consummated at some time in the future. The next day the Methodist church sent an official delegation to the General Assembly asking that they discuss the matter. For several years negotiations were carried on, with the result that in the year 1911 it was decided to take a vote of the Presbyterian church. Before I read the result of that vote, might I say this? In 1905, the union committee appointed by the Presbyterian Assembly made its report

United Church of Canada
Celling of its meeting with the committees of the Methodist and Congregational churches. Among the closing words of that report were these:
It was universally recognized in the joint committee. .	.	.
That is including Methodists, Congrega-tionalists and Presbyterians.
.	.	.	. that a union of the churches to be real and
lasting, must carry the consent of the entire membership.
The assembly adopted that report, sending it forth to the church, and its statements were accepted as the statements adopted by the assembly.
In 1911, however, a vote of the Presbyterian church was taken, the membership at that time including sessions and moderators, being 298,916. Of these, 113,000 voted yea and 50,733 nay. Hon. gentlemen who were in the Private Bills committee and heard Sir Robert Falconer speak on the subject will no doubt remember that, instead of giving the total vote on both sides as well as the full information with regard to that vote, he told us that only 16 per cent of the total vote of the Presbyterian church was against the union in 1911. Let me point out that such a demand is not customary-is quite unusual-in connection with the 'proceedings of any organization. We believe in majority rule in this country; it is the principle which obtains in connection with the management of every organization whether of a religious, a social or a political character. Majority rule is the rule which prevails and absolute unanimity is rarely demanded. So far as the present bill is concerned it has not been apposed by the Methodist church, the Congregational church, or the United committee. That is no new thing. The Methodist church came to parliament for incorporation in 1884. The Presbyterians came for a similar purpose. The Orange society and other bodies came to parliament for incorporation. All the United church is asking for is the right to transact its own business through its own organization. Parliament is not asked to decide any questions of doctrine, or church polity or church government. All the United church asks for is the right to legally transact its own business, and it seems to me we have no right to tell it to go to the courts for a decision. In my opinion parliament would be acting wisely to say to "the supporters of this bill, "We will give you the right, as a United church, to carry on your own affairs and transact your own business." I wish now to proceed along the lines I had been pursuing, and to say a word or two with regard to the national aspect of this question, because a question which involves such a large proportion of the Canadian people does assume a national aspect. It seems to me that the welfare of our country as a whole is involved in this very matter. I should be making a trite remark if I said that Canada was a difficult country to govern; the statement has been made so often as to become commonplace. But the fact remains that whether you consider Canada geographically or economically, to govern it is the despair, I am sure, of all earnest minded statesmen. Now in this proposition to unite the great Protestant churches of this country we have something that may very well make every patriotic Canadian think. In a country like this I think it is very well indeed that we should ,lay emphasis upon those invisible bonds which bind us together in spite of distance, in spite of physical obstacle, in spite of sectional points of view, nay, in spite sometimes of economic differences. I think we Canadian people, we members of parliament, ought to lay stress upon these invisible bonds of citizenship which bind people together in spite of sectional differences and divergent points of view. In this proposition to unite the great Methodist church of this country with the great Presbyterian church, including the Congregational churches, you are creating something that is going to weld this country together from coast to coast. Every connections! officer that travels from ocean to ocean will be a living symbol of the unity of Canada, and the message he will take from one end of Canada to the other will be a message of unity.
I would go a little further, Mr. Chairman, and mention a subject which I believe that

every Canadian, whatever his religious affiliation is, has begun to take very seriously indeed. I refer to the flowing tide of materialism that is swamping this country, in common with other countries, from one coast to the other. We may not look at this thing in the same light, and it is not necessary that we should. Sometimes when on the floor of th-'s House we are dealing with moral questions there is a manifest difference of view between, say, myself and my hon. friends over here; but no matter what the point of view is, the thing viewed is the same, and it is a veiy serious consideration. I have heard sometimes my hon. friends from Quebec, who are of another faith from that of my own, speak very seriously about certain aspects of the moral life of this country, and I have never listened to them except with the greatest of respect, although I may differ from them; and they, in their turn, have listened to me expressing my view as to the moral life of this country, and though they may not have agreed with me in my views, they with me are agreed that the moral life of this country, in common with the moral life of every civilized country, is showing certain marked tendencies which may well cause serious consideration in the minds of all serious-minded citizens. Now what I want to say, Mr. Chairman, is this: Right throughout the length and breadth of this country I want to see a united Protestant church working alongside a united Catholic church, each working within its own sphere, and their spheres are well defined, each working according to its own traditional conception of the problems involved, to maintain as far as they can, and it needs all the effort of both together, in the soul of the Canadian people that reverence for moral sanctions without which no nation can ever prosper. Do not let us bring this subject down to a level where it becomes confused in ancient and petty rivalries. That would be a big mistake.
This is a subject, Mr. Chairman, which while it concerns every patriotic Canadian, concerns primarily I suppose the churches concerned, and it is to be hoped that we as a House will have the greatest possible respect for the expressed will of those great churches, because they have acted in the best interests of those churches; they have acted for their own good. I know it has been hinted, but I think not worthily, that this movement has taken i'ts origin in some overweening ambition on the part of the churches concerned, but I think nothing could be more absurd if you look at the thing fairly. How can this movement which has begun in the spirit of tolerance bear the fruits of intoler-

I have the greatest possible respect for those who are opposed to this bill, but I will tell you, Mr. Chairman, to whom I would go to ask an opinion as to what is for the good of the Presbyteiian church and for the good of the Methodist church in Canada. I would first of all go to the missionaries of those churches who are holding the outposts of Christendom in China and in India, those men who, if any men do at this day, represent the original spirit that created Christianity, those men who, at sacrifice to themselves, are holding fast and firm the principles of Christianity on the outposts of civilization. When you think of names like St. Francis Xavier, Father Damien, Livingstone, Moffat, and Carey, you are recalling men whose names will remain firm in the annals of the race long after the names of our warriors and statesmen have faded away. Those are the men of whom the House ought to be proud, and I would ask the opinion of the living descendants of these men. They have been asked, and what have they said? With almost unanimous voices they have voted in favour of church union. How could they do otherwise? Then I would go to the thousands of ministers who are working in the rural parishes of this country, that great body of Presbyterian and Methodist ministers who are working in the rural fields of this country. They have a right to be asked, because they are bearing the burden and heat of the day, these men who with their families have given their lives to this cause. I know that a good many of our city ministers have generously given their support to this movement, and they are to be honoured for it. But what is the reason? It is because they have been through the mill themselves. They know what it is to work out on some rural charge and to bear the heartache and humiliation of trying to carry on their work in competition with their brother ministers when there was no necessity for that competition-men with the same message, with the same methods, on the same ground, compelled by our denominationalism to carry on their work under those conditions. It is a serious matter, Mr. Chairman.
In this Canada of ours it is becoming more and more difficult to get the young men coming out of our universities to enter the ministry, because they believe our divisions and narrow denominationalism has rendered this sacred calling less than a man's job. Now
this bill which is before us proposes to do away with that obstacle, and to make a thousand parishes, nay, two and three thousand parishes in Canada, a field whereto we can invite our young men to give their life's work. And then I would speak also of the great body of laymen who have to foot the bill. We sometimes talk about the unsupport-ableness of taxes. But people outside the churches know very little about the impost that is laid upon the average church member in trying to carry on work which after all is national work. And I think the laymen of our churches-who are sometimes paying two, three and sometimes four times the amount which they could reasonably be expected to do in order to carry on the work of the congregation-I think those men have a right to be consulted. They have been consulted, and their answer has been overwhelmingly in favour of church union.
I want to say in conclusion that this movement not only commends itself to us from a national point of view, not only from that deference which is due to sister Christian churches endeavouring to carry on a work under very onerous conditions, but also from a strictly legal point of view. The legal side has been almost exclusively discussed this afternoon. I did not enter into it at the beginning, because I thought possibly I might deal with the question from another angle; but I wish to say in conclusion that this bill as introduced is in perfect harmony with the law, as the law is understood by the average lay mind, and contains the most generous provision for minorities. The counsel for the opponents of the bill based his argument, his legal argument, almost exclusively on the Scottish church case. He said in his speech that the principle underlying the Scottish church case was that no general assembly, no matter how unanimous the vote, has the power to destroy the church it was commissioned to preserve. I want to say very respectfully that the learned gentleman when he made that statement was simply filling up a gap in his argument by his forensic imaginings, because there was no such principle embodied in the judgment given. The judgment as laid down by the law lords contained two very clear principles which I ask this House to apply to this case. The first principle was identity of doctrine. The second was that there should be power to change doctrine. They laid upon themselves the onus of proving both and to the satisfaction of themselves, with certain dissentients, they decided that there was no identity of doctrine

-that is, in this specific case there was no identity of doctrine-and there was no power to change doctrine. Those are the two prin-c.ples upon which that case was decided.
Now, I do not need 'to appeal to anyone in particular because it seems to be so plain: Here are these two principles. Let us apply them to the Presbyterian Church in Canada, and let me remark that the Presbyterian Church in Canada is not the Presbyterian Church in Scotland. But let us apply these two principles. First as to identity of doctrine. Well, I have already dealt with that and I did not convert the hon. member for Lunenburg, but I think I showed to the ordinary common sense way of thinking that there is absolutely no difference between the doctrine of the Presbyterian Church in Canada and the doctrine of the Methodist Church in Canada-absolutely no difference. They teach the children out of the same text books in the Sunday schools; the missionaries divide the work between them, signifying that no longer have they the consciousness of any special message to deliver; and they use also each others parsonages, and no doubt they borrow each other's money. Now, leaving all technicalities aside, I do not think that any man can stand up here and say that the doctrine, the working doctrine, of these churches is in any way different; they are absolutely identical.
But then, what about the power to change doctrine? Well, with regard to the Presbyterian Church in Canada I might, perhaps, endeavour to enlighten the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler)) if he were here; but he is not here. If he were here I might tell him that the Presbyterian Church in Canada, whatever was the position of the uniting churches in Scotland, has the right to change its doctrine. That right is set forth in a very clear legal decision that was given in the Dobbie case. That right is couched in unmistakable terms in the rules and usages of the church; that right has been exercised in two specific instances; and what is more, that right is stamped indelibly upon the consciousness of the Presbyterian church in this country. Well, if that is the case, if we have identity in doctrine, if we have power to change doctrine, why should this parliament confront the Presbyterian church with the technicalities it is trying to get away from?
With respect to this amendment I could have understood the member for Lunenburg, and others, if they had attempted to get a vote against the petition. If they had come

straight out against the petitioners in the first place and said "This bill must not go through this House" I could have understood it. But they bring in this amendment, and they have very cunningly laid a snare before the members of this House. What they despaired of doing in the open light of public discussion they thought they could do at a subsequent date in the twilight of legal disputation. They remind me of a carnivorous wasp which never kills its prey outright but just-sticks in its probe at the right place and waits for another day to finish the job. I cannot understand an attempt of that kind to mislead this House, for after all the intention and the motive behind the amendment is to defeat the bill and that is all there is to it. If this parliament yields to the amendment it will be shirking a duty, a clear duty, which belongs to it; a duty which the British parliament just two or three years ago accepted in the Scottish church bill. The very thing these petitioners arl asking us to do this evening is the thing which the Scottish church asked the British House of Commons to do three years ago, and the British House of Commons did it without demur. They did it in deference to the expressed will of a great Scottish church; aind if the thing that is expedient and right for the British parliament to do is wrong and inexpedient for us to do, then I fail to understand the situation at all.
And then, Mr. Chairman, finally, if this parliament accedes to the movers of this amendment they will be, as I have already indicated, taking away from the church the responsibility that rests within the church, that has always rested within the church, and which no church in Canada would consciously allow to pass out of its hands. They are taking this matter which concerns doctrine and policy, the most sacred right of all Christian bodies, and wresting it out of the sacred realm to which it belongs, and they are hurling it ruthlessly and thoughtlessly into the maelstrom of political controversy. I appeal to the House with the very highest of motives not to accede to the individuals who have been pressing this matter upon us for some weeks, but to accede to those who have sent them here, and to accede in particular to the great Presbyterian church as that church has expressed itself through its historic General Assembly, and has expressed itself so decisively and so finally only about a week ago.

There are several subjects which I will refer to before dealing with the amendments as such, because there are several incorrectly stated propositions and certain misunderstandings in the matter. First of all, a word on the subject of union. All anti-unionists are favourable to uniion. I have said that and I repeat it. They are favourable to union, and not only so but it is their duty to favour union in so far as possible. That being the case, all Methodists, all Congregationalists, and such Presbyterians as so desire, are free tomorrow to enter into the union. And under what circumstances will they obtain more Presbyterians because it is evident that Presbyterians will remain out of the union and that the Presbyterian church will continue. I say it is some obsession on the word "union" in the case that prevents a settlement on the point. As I say, we are favourable to union, but we are not favourable to union beyond the rights of those who are petitioning, nor are we favourable to the proposal to interfere with the rights of those who are opposed to it. We are not favouring union at the expense of taking away a church which we consider belongs to those who wish to retain it. We are not favourable to a union compelling a large number of
people to go into a church who are not willing to do so. It is one of the great principles that comes to us, one of the great heritages, that we have not only civil but religious liberty. It is no use saying "This is a great idea, therefore go to it." It must be dependent on the circumstances, and must be dependent on people's own desires. Each one must judge for himself. It is a common saying that union is a good thing; the bill is for union; vote for it. That is altogether subject to various conditions. Are the petitioning churches entitled to it, or have they authority to ask for it Have they authority to do away with their own church? Is it right to put into that church people who are not prepared to go there? Those are important questions. If there something that is more important than union, it is the principle of religious freedom.
The next point I desire to refer to is the question of majorities, and there is a good deal of misunderstanding on that subject. First, let me say that the General Assembly does not represent the sentiment of the people, and I will try to demonstrate that in a moment or two. The General Assembly does not represent the sentiment of the people, nor do the votes of the General Assembly authorize the General Assembly to enter into union. And all I am saying, or nearly all I propose to say, is from the Presbyterian standpoint, because that is the section that is entering the protest. The union movement in the Presbyterian church was what? It was clerical and official; it never arose from the people. The explanation of the twenty years taken with the proceedings is the best evidence that it never received the support of the people as a whole. As I say, it was official and clerical. Therefore that influence has naturally had a great restraining influence on the people, and in the process of time, when they saw especially the nature of the bill that is before us now, they broke through the influence and control of the clergy. It is not now possible to say which is the majority.
The General Assembly does not represent the sentiment of the people, because it is not in any sense representative in numbers. A congregation, no matter how small, if it has only a score or two score members, has its minister and elder in presbytery and a congregation of two thousand has its minister and elder in presbytery. Now, two thousand members in one part of the church may thus have only two representatives in the presbytery, and two thousand people in other places may have two hundred representatives in the presbytery, and those representatives

Let me say a word about the union of 1875 which has been frequently quoted as a justification for the proposed union of to-day. The union of 1875 was a union of four Presbyterian churches, not different denominations, not different churches. When I say that it was a union, that is not quite an accurate term. It was a reunion. Those churches had formerly been one and they came together again. That is one difference and a very vital substantial difference it is. But there are others. Those Presbyterian churches were not incorporated. The Presbyterian church of to-day is not incorporated. There is no need of its being incorporated. Another difference is that when that union took place, the congregations that decided to go in went in, and those that decided to remain out-and they were not many-remained out. What became of those congregations that remained out? Were they east adrift as isolated congregations without their church? Not at all. They remained in their mother church. In Pictou, especially, where they decided not to go in, there was formed for the two presbyteries a synod in which the church continued in connection with the mother church, the Church of Scotland. There was no taking away of their church from those people, and one of the great difficulties and hardships at the present day is the threat of their church being taken away from the people.

The British act of 1921 did not give the Church of Scotland the power to abandon its Presbyterian standards; any changes in doctrine which it authorized had to be in harmony with the fundamental doctrines of the church as laid down at the Scottish Reformation, and as indicated in article 5. It would never have authorized such changes as appeared in the basis of union. The fact that legislation was necessary for the Church of Scotland indicates that without such legislation the Church of Scotland had no power to institute any change. The Presbyterian Church in Canada never obtained any such power from any parliament, but the church courts assumed to have that authority and, what is more, exercised it without any prior legislative sanction. The promoters of the bill before the Private Bills committee asserted and attempted to sustain the position that all that had been done by the church courts had been legally done and within the competence of such courts. Any action of the church courts in Canada was taken long before the legislation of 1921 was enacted, so that those actions could not have been based upon that precedent. In any event the British legislation of 1921 has no application to Canada and should not influence our decision.
Now I come to the two great objections to which I think the bill is open, and the first is that the action of the General Assembly is unconstitutional. And it seems to me there is a great deal of confusion on this point. I notice that some hon. members speak of the General Assembly as if it were the church, while others refer to it as a corporate body with certain functions. We shall see in a moment what the extent of its functions is. When the union of the four Presbyterian churches in Canada took place in 1875 those churches united under what was called the basis of union, and therein it is stated that the scriptures shall be the infallible rule of faith, and the Westminster Confession of Faith the subordinate standard; and then reference is made to the form of Presbyterian church government and "The directory for the public worship of God." That is the basis of union and the basis of their faith I want the committee to consider also what vows the min-
isters have taken in entering that church. They sign a vow that they believe in the Westminster Confession of Faith as adopted by this church in the basis of union, and the government of the church by sessions, presbyteries, synods and general assemblies, to be founded on and agreeable to the word of God; that they own the purity of worship at present authorized by this church and that they engage to adhere faithfully to the doctrine of the said confession, to maintain and defend the said government, to conform to the said worship, to submit to the discipline of the church. And then listen to these words:
To follow no divisive course from, the present order established therein.
The elders take a somewhat similar vow when they are ordained. Now, what is laid down for the General Assembly to do? The General Assembly receives and disposes of petitions, overtures, references, complaints, and so on; prescribes and regulates the course of duty of students having the ministry in view; corresponds with other churches, and so on; reviews the records of synods, deals with matters respecting doctrine, worship, discipline and government of the church. Its duty also is "to preserve the unity of the church;" that seems to have been overlooked in the recent years. Now, in view of what I have read-and all these things must be considered together: the basis of uni on; the vows of the ministers and elders of the church, their duties and the duties of the General Assembly as laid down in the Rules of Procedure-is there any authority to abolish their church? In all that I have read is there the remotest suggestion to that effect? On the contrary, the requirement to maintain and defend the church and to follow no divisive course therefrom is clearly laid down, and there is the requirement also to accept the Confession of Faith. There is every authority for the continuance of this church, but in my humble opinion there is no authority for its extinction. The General Assembly is not the church; it is a committee of the church to carry on the church's business affairs.
Now, a word about the free church case because two things are clearly shown. First of all, in the General Assembly no vote, no majority vote, not even a unanimous vote, can destroy the church that it is its commission to serve. Mark these words: No majority, not even a unanimous vote, can abolish the church. That is an entirely different view from what we have heard this afternoon. What does it mean? It means that the General Assembly has no authority to disturb the continuity of the church. The General Assembly

is merely a committee carrying on the business of the church, acting within its vows, dealing with matters affecting internal management. It is beyond its power and its authority to destroy the church which by their vows they have undertaken to serve and to maintain. There is a good deal of loose talk about this question of trusts. I have heard a man say, "Oh, well, it was a good many years ago that that condition was laid down; you really do not need to carry it out." Surely an attitude of that kind is no less blamable than any departure from the rigid interpretation of a will. The conditions surrounding the disposition of these properties must be scrupulously carried out.
I do not propose to read many quotations, but I would like to read from a decision of Lord Lindley of the Privy Council in the Wee Free case. This is what he said.
If, therefore, a synod or council, under colour of exercising their authority, were to destroy the church which they were appointed to preserve, or were to abrogate the doctrines which they were appointed to maintain, their acts would be ultra vires and invalid in point of law, and it would ibe the duty of every court in the United Kingdom so to hold, if the question ever involved a controversy as to civil rights and so arose for judicial decision.
In other words, this matter of union is not a question of preference. Somebody gets up and says this is the greatest thing that eve" happened, but that is not enough; that will not do. We know that union has been set aside in Australia, in New Zealand and South Africa; we must have regard to the facts. This so-called sweep towards union has not gone on; it has fallen through. The unanimous decision of the Privy Council in the case to which I 'have referred was that churches must have identical doctrines to unite. Two of the Privy Council held that there was no difference, but on the question of law they all agreed. Two said there was no difference, and five said there was.
I want to remind the committee that there is a legal action pending in the Ontario courts. If the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) carries, then an opportunity of continuing the action in the Ontario courts will be lost to the anti-unionists. Is that a fair and proper thing? Is this matter so urgent as to take away the right of these people to have their case decided in the Ontario courts? And even if it were urgent, is it right and proper, is it just, to do anything else than to see that this action is allowed to proceed at law?
227*
I want to refer to a few subjects that have been mentioned by those who are in favour of union. It is stated by the unionists that all constitutional steps have been taken. A great many steps have been taken, no doubt, and so far as they go I presume they are constitutional. But on what basis do they rest? They are a series of steps resting in the air. You must have a basic authority for your procedure. You may proceed to the presbytery and from there through the various stages to the synod and to the assembly; that sort of performance is constitutional enough- provided that the General Assembly has the necessary power . The basic question is have they that power? That is what is in dispute. I venture to say that what I have stated makes out a strong case, but I do not wish to make other men accept that; let us have the question settled where it can best be settled, and that is in a higher civil court.
I would say also that the General Assembly has no power to transfer to another church property which has been given for a specific purpose. That is a breach of trust. That is a matter that should also be sent to the courts. Does the committee consider it a proper thing to decide on the question of a very large trust fund, the existence of a church and the happiness of hundreds of thousands of devout people in this way in the House of Commons? Or does it not appear to the ordinary common sense man that this matter should be sent to the courts, where it can be argued out fully pro and con, and a decision be taken which I submit under all ordinary circumstances cannot be as fairly and as properly and sanely arrived at in this committee. To those who are interested in legal cases I would mention a Canadian case, Anderson versus Gislason. That was a Manitoba case concerned with the union of two churches, but the Presbyterian church was not involved. Legal action was taken, and this is what the appeal judge, Judge Dennistoun, said:
The guarantee of religious freedom has nothing to do with the property. It does not guarantee freedom to steal churches. It secures to individuals the right of withdrawing, forming a new society, with such creed and government as they please, but it does not confer on them the right of taking the property consecrated to other uses by those who may now be sleeping in their graves.
That is a Canadian case. I said that the first great objection to the bill was that the General Assembly has not the power to do what it is attempting to do. Secondly, parliament has not the power to pass the bill. Can parliament incorporate and merge together people who do not wish to be merged? Is that not an infringment of the liberty of the
United Church of Canada

subject, which will not be allowed under the British North America Act? And so with regard to incorporated congregations that have not asked and do not wish to go into the union; and so as to the diversion of trust funds, which is provincial property. There are some important quotations in this connection in the Free church case which I shall not detain the committee to read, although they are in strong support of what I am saying, and would well repay any one who chooses to read them. They are to be found in the judgments of Lord Halsbury, the Lord Chancellor, and Lord Alverstone Chief Justice of England.
It is also said there is no need of this conditional clause in the amended bill, that is the clause I am speaking of as being ultra vires of parliament. There is no need of such a clause in the bill, it is said, as action can be taken in any case. Of course, it can be taken in any case. Does anybody suppose it could not? We all know that it could be taken. But it has been pointed out to the committee that it was urged that parliament- bad not the authority to pass this bill, and strong reasons were given in support of that contention. Is parliament then prepared to-shut its eyes to that and go on and effect union, and then let somebody else attempt and perhaps succeed in upsetting the action of parliament? Is that justice, is that equity, to those who are protesting against this bill? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is only proper and fair and just that this question of the authority of parliament be settled before the bill is brought into force, if it should pass this House. There is no use in saying that can be done some time. It is the duty of parliament to see that that provision is in the act.
Furthermore, there is no need of incorporation. The Presbyterian Church in Canada is not incorporated. There is nothing to prevent this union we are speaking of taking place without incorporation. Why is that not done? I will give you the only possible explanation, and that is that such a union as they are asking parliament for could not otherwise take place, because the courts would not allow it any more than they did in the Free church case. The courts would not allow the transfer of property and trusts, and that is why they are coming to parliament and asking for a power which I do not think they could obtain in the civil courts of the land.
It is stated that passing the bill as it now stands-it was stated only a few moments ago-would not settle the matter. Certainly not. Whoever expected it would settle the matter? The only course then would be to

come back with an amended bill. This bill should not pass in my view, because it would not settle the matter. Let them come back with an amended bill, and it would go through. But when a man says: Pass this bill because it is coming up again next year, does he mean to say-and this is the only interpretation- give him the bill to keep him quiet, to please him, or whatever you like, so that he does not come back to parliament. Give him the bill granting him powers and privileges that he does not possess and that takes away powers and the church from others, just to satisfy him. Surely the committee will not approve, cannot approve of any such iniquity as that; and that is what it all means. I can understand the committee would be very glad indeed if they could get rid of this question, if they could, free our House and these corridors of a great deal of solicitude that has been shown all the members during the last few weeks. They would do a great deal to do that, but we cannot get rid of it at the expense of people's rights, and that is what we are doing if we go on any such argument as has been placed before us. Then it is said that if the General Assembly had not the necessary power, the passing of this act would give the supplementary and additional power necessary. Is that the way we wish to treat those who come to parliament protesting that this union is against their rights and that their church is being seized? I think not, Mr. Chairman. Again, it asked, why was legal action not taken before? And because it was not taken before, it is argued that parliament cannot be expected to wait. I have heard this said several times. It implies that the action of the petitioners has been dilatory. It implies that they have delayed so that this matter can be held up. I have taken the opportunity of asking Mr. Chrysler, who I think is certainly a man of repute in this community, to give some facts in this connection, and this is what he says:
Some question has been raised as to whether proceedings in the action of Cunningham et al vs. Pidgeon et al should not have been taken at an earlier date.
That is in reference to Bill No. 47.
I was asked before the Private Bills committee, with regard to the time taken in commencing the action, but I understood from the questions then asked that the time referred to was that between the publication of the notice of application to parliament and the issuing of the writ. I explained then that there was only the necessary time occupied in the preparation of the statement of claim and the printing thereof.
I understand now that it is said that the present plaintiff (or some plaintiff) might have proceeded at any time after the passing of the resolutions by the General Assembly adopted on the 11th day of June, 1923, which are quoted in paragraph 37 of the plaintiff's statement of claim.

United Church oj Canada
I am pleased to have the opportunity of placing this matter before the committee because I think it meets the many criticisms that have been repeatedly made on this point. Mr. Chrysler goes on to say:
If this view were correct it might lead to the conclusion that an action should have been commenced at any time after the resolutions adopted by the assembly in 1916, which are in substance very similar to those of 1923. (paragraph 29 of the statement of claim).
In each case there is the assertion of the intention to take very bold and definite action by the assembly, qualified in each case by the condition that no such action should be final until confirmed by legislation.
This matter was very carefully considered, and in my view no action could be maintained in a court of law merely because resolutions had been adopted by the General Assembly, or other courts of the church, which might or might not be acted upon or be repealed or modified by a subsequent meeting of the assembly.
The resolutions of 1916 and 1923 were each of them, upon their face, provisional and conditional upon legislation being obtained.
The resolution of 1923 affirms the decision of the assembly:
"To proceed forthwith to the consummation of union upon the terms of the draft bills, which are hereby approved in principle and generally as to form as necessary to give legal effect to the said union, and to furnish the United church with legal authority requisite to corporate action and as by said bills provided."
These proceedings are set out in paragraphs 37 to 50 inclusive of the statement of claim, and the notice of application to parliament in paragraph 56.
The action was commenced as soon after notice of application to parliament had been given as practicable, the proceeding being one in which it was convenient and proper, according to practice, to provide for the service of the statement of claim along with the writ of summons, as several of the defendants were not resident in the province of Ontario, the legislation was intended to terminate the existence of tihe Presbyterian Church in Canada by merging it in a new statutory corporation, and to invade the constitutional rights and property of the church and its corporate bodies holding property, provincial and local, and to take away the congregational property held in perpetuity in trust for the use of the members of the Presbyterian church.
Until the representatives and agents of the assembly themselves applied to the civil power to enforce their resolutions, either by action in court, or by applying for legislation, any action taken to test the pretended powers of the assembly would, I think, have been premature.
The decisive step, taken to enforce the resolution of the assembly, was first taken when the notice of application to parliament was published.
Yours truly,
F. H. Chrysler.

Will the hon. member not admit that when Mr. Chrysler was under crossexamination he made the statement "I have not had time to examine this bill; this bill is beyond my comprehension", and that Mr. Mason, the solicitor for the union party, made a straightforward and honourable statement of the matter?

No, I do not admit
anything of the kind. It is also stated that
the amendment whidh has been made to the bill in section 2 is an evasion. If ever a fair or honourable amendment was introduced into a bill it is the one that was inserted before the Private Bills committee. It says in effect "You can have your bill, but if there is any doubt as to the constitutional powers of the General Assembly the question must be submitted to the courts". What can be more fair or more honourable than that? Where is the evasion? I think the man who says there is evasion in that shows symptons of astigmatism if you know what that is.
Explain please?

The Minister of Railways is so well informed that I need not explain the term to him.
Summing up I ask what is the position now of the Presbyterian church? Notwithstanding official pronouncements at the early stages of union negotiations that practical unanimity would be essential, in spite of steadily increasing opposition so that now probably one-half the church is opposed to union, in spite of there being no vote for nine years, and that over 100,000 new members have joined the church since the last vote, regardless of the assembly failing in any fair measure to represent the people, regardless of the power of the General Assembly being challenged as its constitutional authority in seeking union and there being strong evidence to support that step; regardless that the power of parliament itself is distinctly disputed, and that the existence of the church of thousands of devout people is threatened-with all these facts before us an amendment is presented to eliminate section 2 which would mean, if the bil'i is passed along with it, that there is not only confiscation and coercion but infringement of religious liberty. I think it may be said of those who are in favour of union that they have "followed too much the devices and desires of their own hearts". They see this ideal before them. They think that what they are striving for will be the solution of everything. They are pressing towards that goal without due regard to the liberties and rights of others, without vouchsafing to other people the right to choose and worship as they think best. There is no use in attempting to tell anybody how they must worship; what they should do in regard to religious matters. That is an impossible idea. The question is now before us for settlement, and surely this parliament is not going to dictate to any body of people as to what church they should belong.
United Church oj Canada

I would like to make a few remarks on this bill. In the debate so far this afternoon and this evening, this matter has been very ably and very fully discussed. I had the honour of being chairman of the Private Bills committee to which the bill was referred. As several hon. members have mentioned, for many years no private bill has caused such a tremendous interest as is taken in this measure. The committee gave both sides a very fair and full hearing. Six days were occupied in presenting the case to the committee. The arguments were well presented from both sides. While there was keen feeling in the matter, there is no question that courtesy and kindness were shown on both sides, and that was only to be expected from men of such high standing in the church, at the bar and among the laity. The committee discussed this bill for the equivalent of another four days, and went into the question very carefully.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Methodist and Congregational churches are practically unanimous in asking for this church union bill, but gentlemen appeared before the committee and presented a very grave difference of opinion on the part of communicants and members of the Presbyterian church. They claimed that the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church had not the legal and constitutional right to enter into such an agreement with the other churches. Excluding this question which is now before the committee in regard to the amendment of my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown), I think the remaining provisions of the bill were very carefully considered and thought out, and practically follow what was asked for by the promoters of the 'bill. But on the question of this amendment to the preamble and section 2 which is now sought to be eliminated, the committee felt- and I agree with the committee-that there was grave doubt as to whether the Presbyterian General Assembly had the right to enter into this agreement.
I am not going to enter into a long legal argument, but I would like to draw the attention of the committee to the questions which are raised in the case of Cunningham versus Pidgeon, which is now before the Ontario courts. The case mentioned subsection 1 of section 2 of this bill. The reason that I am going to read some of the points presented in that case is that these were the points that were brought before the committee and argued, and are on record in this case

in the courts of Ontario. Another reason why I read from this record is that I desire to show that there is a grave doubt, to put it fairly, and I want to show, Mr. Chairman, that the questions which are involved in this case are questions of doctrine and faith, which hon. members who are for this amendment said the committee and parliament should not discuss, the point being that these legal and religious questions should be submitted to the courts of the land, to men who are trained to consider these very questions, trained to weigh the evidence and to take these matters in hand. Paragraph 63 of this statement of claim reads:
The covenant of the Presbyterian church in 1875 and its constitution and rule contain no provision for any alteration being made in the principles of the said church or for union with any oilier church or association of Christians holding different principles.
Paragraph 64 reads:
The plaintiffs further submit that the said assembly had not, nor has any assembly of the Presbyterian church, power to appoint delegates or any committee of delegates or agents to apply for legislation designed and intended to annihilate the identity and continuity of the Presbyterian churoh by merging it in a new corporation and to bring about the alienation or spoliation of the property of the church, nor to take proceedings to procure the conveyance by act of parliament or legislatures of such property to Buch new corporation.
Paragraph 66 reads:
The plaintiffs submit that it is not withiin the power of the courts of the Presbyterian church or any combination of them, or of any majority of its officers or members to alter or vary the trusts upon which the property vested in or acquired by it, or by trustees for it, is held, or to alter the purposes for which it was founded and established.
That refers more particularly to subsection 2 in regard to the constitutionality, which was referred to by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). Then I turn to paragraph 86, which is purely one in regard to doctrine, and reads:
