In place of the standards of the Presbyterian church, namely the Confession of Faith, which is % statement of a system of doctrine, an the form of a creed or covenant, and the longer and shorter catechisms, provided for the instruction of its members the proposed basis of the United church substitutes a statement which purports to set forth not the creed of the church but the substance of the Christian faith as commonly held among us.
There is a question solely of doctrine or creed or faith, which I submit should go to the courts. Then I refer to paragraph 96 which reads:
The plaintiffs submit that the twenty articles which follow the preamble are not identical with, but a departure from the doctrine of the Presbyterian church as set forth in its standards.

United Church oj Canada
Paragraph 101 reads:
The following differences and departures from the Westminster Confession of Faith in the proposed basis of union are set forth in the opposing statements or propositions which follow:
And here are ten very grave differences of opinion on doctrine as between the United church and the Presbyterians. I maintain that these are not questions which should be settled by a committee or by parliament, but are questions which should be decided by the courts of the land. Paragraph 102 recites these ten grave differences which I will not repeat, and states further:
The above instances do not constitute the whole sum of the differences between the Confession of Faith and the basis of union, but are given only to illustrate the opposition between these two documents not only in their superficial features but even more in their fundamental conceptions.
In other words, there appears to be a vast difference in regard to the two conceptions as regards doctrine and faith. At a meeting subsequent to the General Assembly of 1923, a reply was presented by those in favour of union to the dissent of those gentlemen who opposed union, and as appears on page 9, the chairman of that committee in his report said amongst other things in section (2):
This assembly maintains that the General Assembly held in Winnipeg in 1916 did act within its rights and powers in approving of the said basis of union.
(3) The assembly denies that its acts in this behalf are illegal, and denies that it has in effect seceded from the Presbyterian Church in Canada.
Section (5) reads:
The assembly, claiming that its acts have been legal and within its powers and rights, holds that those who dissent from this deliverance and not the majority are the parties responsible for this threatened schism in the church and for any consequence which may flow therefrom.
In other words, they joined issue in regard to the legality of the proceedings of the assembly. When the gentlemen appeared before the committee, they argued that the General Assembly had acted in a legal and constitutional manner in carrying this out. It is true that the case of Overtoun and the Free Church of Scotland has been cited before the committee, and I will only mention the fact that the decision apparently was directly against the General Assembly to make any particular change in doctrine. The gentlemen who appeared before the committee in favour of union said that they could differentiate this legislation from the Free Church case. All that I am concerned in showing from these statements is, first, that there was a serious doubt as to the right of the General Assembly; secondly, that parliament and this committee are not the authorities to decide questions of
doctrine and of faith, and that such questions should go to the proper tribunals set apart by the constitution of this country, namely the law courts of the land.
When were the law courts set apart to decide questions of faith and doctrine?

This question has
arisen between parties in the Presbyterian church under their own system of government, under the laws and obligations laid down in the church, and, therefore, any question of dispute which would arise between one section of that church and the other, any legal rights that they would have, would have to be tried by the courts. If the question of doctrine comes into this question, it would naturally be tried by the courts as was the case in the Overtoun case.
The Barrier Act has been referred to. The Barrier Act is simply an act of the Presbyterian Church in Canada which is used as a check of legislation. The General Assembly passes a law, and then it is sent down during the following year to the different presbyteries for assent or dissent before it is put into effect. But it does not give any additional power to the General Assembly as regards legislation outside of whatever rights and powers it may have.
I would have thought that the reference to the Supreme court would be welcomed by the promoters of this bill, because there is no doubt that in this legislation we are dealing with property and civil rights in the provinces, with education in the provinces and with trusts in the provinces. It is true that legislation has been obtained from many of the provinces and legislation is still to be obtained in two or three more. But the point I attempt to make is this, that if the question is referred to the Supreme court, this will prevent litigation in the other provincial courts of this country until the Supreme court has decided whether the legislation we have granted is ultra vires or not. This will save money to both sides and it will save delay by having the matter referred. I have supported and I am supporting the report of the committee, but the question of delay was brought up. The committee tried to meet that point in the reference to the courts by limiting the time to two years. But if a reference of both of those legal questions in subsections 1 and 2 of section 2 to the Supreme court is put forward, as it is following the principle adopted by the committee, I would agree to it because it would avoid delay and expense. I am in favour of church
United Church of Canada

union, but I think that in granting church union you cannot take away whatever legal rights may belong to the minority in the Presbyterian church.
The question of the General Assembly has been touched upon. I have a great respect for the opinion of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church and for the system of church government; but the gentlemen who make up the General Assembly are elders appointed for life. They go to the General Assembly, and in all honour, without any question of their good faith, they have a perfect right to vote for or against church union as they see fit whether their congregation is in favour of union or not. The point I wish to make is that they are not instructed by the congregation to make a direct vote.	Why did the
General Assembly, I suppose in its wisdom, ask for a vote in 1911 and again in 1915? Surely it was to get that advice from the great mass of communicants and members of their church. In the last vote of 1915, out of 336,822 communicants, 106,534 voted for church union and 69,000 against it. That meant about one third of the communicants of the Presbyterian church. Now, there is a general law in this country governing corporations providing that when any serious move is made, in order to protect the minority, there shall be a two thirds vote of the shareholders. I would not go quite so far as that in this matter, but all that is shown as regards the democracy of this question is that nine years ago one third of the communicants of the Presbyterian church voted in favour of union. We are the representatives of the people and it seems to me it would have been of great assistance to us, even apart from the legal aspect of the matter, if a vote had' been taken at a later date than 1915.
As has been stated this afternoon and repeated over and over again during the past few weeks, the state cannot interfere with religion. I want to read a statement from a pamphlet entitled "Parliament and the Church" addressed to members of parliament by Professor R. E. Welsh, D.D. of the Presbyterian College, Montreal. He says:
Pari Lament is not a court of appeal from the churches upon any ecclesiastical matter. Their creeds or any modifications therein, and their procedure according to their constitution, are determined solely by themselves as free, self-governing religious communities, having neither political nor commercial aims and uses. Any intrusion upon the action of General Assembly,

General Conference, or other church court, in respect of its own functions, would be a violation of the sacred principle of the spiritual independence of the church of Christ and would never be endured in a free country.
Well, I agree with that, with this important addition that as between the members of their own communities or sects or religions the governing body of the church has acted legally according to the agreement or the basis upon which they all join. It is for that reason that I believe in referring this question to the courts. If you accept the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and you forbid any reference of the matter to the courts you are deciding a religious question without any consideration for the minority, the thousands of communicants of the Presbyterian church who are opposed to union, and that I maintain would be an interference on the part of this body with the religious opinions of a large section of the Presbyterian church in this country. For that reason and for others which I have advanced I will support my committee and vote against the amendment of my hon. friend from Lisgar.

The hon. gentleman makes no reference to an important contingency. Suppose that through a technicality the courts should decide that the procedure of the General Assembly was not in order; how does he provide for the carrying out of what is practically the unanimous will of the Methodist and Congregational churches and those Presbyterians who want union? The nature of the bill denies the possibility of union to those large numbers who are in favour of it.

If the decision of the
courts were 'against the action of the General Assembly it would then be the duty of parliament to meet the situation. There has been a great deal of talk in regard to the remedial legislation passed in connection with the Free church. That decision, as has been pointed out, left a very small minority, so small that a commission was appointed to inquire into the question, and it was that commission that decided that the trusts of the church and the management of its affairs could not be carried out by those who were legally entitled to the control of that body. It was then that the commission advised parliament to pass a law covering that contingency. I understand that in that case it was found that one-third of those who were by law declared to be the rightful members of the church were entitled to take all the

United Church of Canada
property. I say therefore that the question would have to be settled by the courts. This legidation provides that, if the General Assembly acted in a legal and constitutional maner, then the bill should become effective.

That is not the point.
Having provided in the bill for many contingencies so as to obviate any repetition of this controversy, which is not in the interests of the churches, of religion, or the welfare of the country, why not
10	p.m. go further and provide for another very important contingency? If the courts should decide that the procedure of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church was not in order, should not the remaining bodies who wish the union be free to unite? Why is that provision omitted from the bill?

I do not see how
you can arrange for a contingency of that kind until the matter has been settled in the courts and you know where you stand.
When this bill was before the committee why did the hon. member refuse to hear counsel that was opposed to the amendment when he heard counsel on each and every one of the other sections in the bill?

That is easily
answered; after the public hearing it was decided by the committee that we should not hear any outside the committee on the preamble, and I was simply carrying out that arrangement as I did in every instance.

Counsel for the union
came to me and requested me to obtain for him the right to be heard on that question before the vote was taken.

It is not my intention to speak at any great length on the question before the chair. Since the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin), has expressed his views, I should feel inclined to refrain from saying anything whatever on the subject, as I find myself fully in accord with what he has stated in his speech. Every opportunity was given by the chairman of the committee to both parties to the controversy to make the fullest statement of their case. I feel that every member of the committee gave the most careful consideration to the evidence that was offered. When the amendment that now appears in the bill was moved by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) I took occasion to second it after
giving a good deal of thought to the matter, and I do not think that this House is commissioned to revise or repeal the decision of that committee. Every phase of the question was fully argued in the committee by the ablest counsel who could be procured.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would like to direct
the attention of the committee-not particularly of the hon. member who is speaking- to a reference in Bourinot which I fear may be disregarded in connection with this discussion.
I quote from page 357:
Neither can a member, in speaking, refer to anything said or done in a previous debate during the same session-a rule necessary to economize the time of the House, and a restraint upon members to prevent them from reviving a debate already concluded. Neither is it regular to refer to arguments used in committee of the whole, nor to any amendment proposed in the same.
I do not suggest that the hon. member is disobeying or disregarding that rule, but from some comments that have been made I fear there is a danger that it may be disregarded. If the hon. member will excuse the interruption, I simply want to draw that to the attention of the committee.

I have no intention of
repeating any part of the argument presented by counsel to the committee; I merely mention the fact that argument was made before the committee, without stating what it was. As I have suggested, the House is not conditioned to determine the question now before us as the committee was conditioned to determine it. The committee had all the evidence before them; they had an opportunity of discussing it among themselves and of considering it fully. This House has never had that evidence before it and therefore has had no opportunity of weighing it. Nor has the House had the advantage of the arguments of counsel made before the committee. It seems to me that the safest thing for the House to do is to rely upon the action of the committee. The House cannot, upon the arguments presented here this afternoon and to-night, undertake to decide on the matters involved; that cannot be intelligently done unless all the evidence and all the arguments are taken into consideration. So that to ask this House to undertake to annul or repeal what the committee has done seems to me, in the circumstances, to be asking the House to do altogether too much.
Before this bill was brought into parliament there wa,s an action pending, and the fact that that action is pending is the strongest possible evidence of the bona fides of those who instituted that action. On the other hand those
United Church of Canada

who are promoting this union bill are endeavouring to get through the House a reversal of the opinion of the committee and to stifle the litigation to that extent, to prevent those who have confidence in their action from having it properly brought before the courts and adjudicated upon. They would have this House, which has not the information, the argument or the evidence before it, pass legislation that -would altogether wipe that provision out of the bill. That does not seem to indicate the same amount of good faith or of confidence on their part in the success of their cause as is exhibited by those who have taken the action and are now maintaining it before the courts.
Is there a real bona fide question involved in the motion now before the committee? Can this parliament, can this committee say that there is no question to be determined by the courts? No doubt it has the power to do so, but will any hon. member say that no question is involved in this bill that is in controversy between the parties and that ought not to be settled-settled by the courts, if you will? If there is such a question, then is this parliament going to aid the one in evading litigation or assist the other in succeeding in the litigation? The fairest possible course parliament could take is to maintain the statu quo between the two parties, leaving each his own rights to be determined upon the evidence in the way that matters of that kind are usually determined.
I am in favour of voluntary union of the churches, but I am not in favour of compulsory union, and I cannot think I ever will be. I do not think the greatest good comes from compulsory union in anything, and that applies to churches as well as to anything else. If this church union is to be compulsory, they cannot expect to get from it the benefits that would otherwise accrue if it were a voluntary measure. Now while that is so, there is this question between the two: The unionists say: We have no desire and no intention, and we have never attempted, to coerce those who do not want to become unionists. On the other hand, the anti-unionists say: You are by this bill compelling us to do something we do not want to do. Now there is the issue. How are you going to determine it? Is parliament going to say the anti-unionists are right, or is parliament going to say that those who are in favour of union are right? Is parliament going to determine that question at all? Is not that a question that is right and proper, and that should only be decided by the courts of the land constituted for that purpose?

I have spoken longer than I intended. I merely want to repeat, the committee was in a position to decide this matter, to protect the rights of minorities, and if there is a fundamental principle of British government, it is that the rights of minorities must be protected. That is -what the committee was in a position to do in this matter. Will parliament undertake to say that they were wrong in doing that, and deprive the minority of their rights as determined in the courts?

As a member of the Private Bills committee I have been trying to analyze the somewhat extensive evidence which has been placed before us in the past few weeks. I propose very briefly to outline some of the main points as they appeal to me, not merely from the legal standpoint, but from that of the wider aspects of the case. The heart of the bill, I take it, is contained in the words of the preamble, that the three churches desire to unite "without loss of their identity." That little phrase is the very key to the whole situation. It is that which causes the greater part of the controversy. The churches claim the right to unite without the loss of their identity. The petitioners came to parliament in the first place, we are told, in order that they might avoid litigation. In this apparently they have been disappointed, as the case is now before the Ontario courts. They make the claim that the steps which have been taken towards union have been taken constitutionally, that is, as provided by the regulations of the various churches concerned, and I think that their claim along that line has not been successfully disputed.
They claim secondly that they have made provision for non-concurring congregations. I might say that certain modifications that were made in committee make it clear that no one was to be forced to go into the union but rather that he might stay out. That announcement seemed to clear that point somewhat. Moreover it is pointed out by the advocates of the union that there is provision for the division of general church property; that is, colleges and certain trust funds of various kinds that are general in character, and are controlled by the church at large. It would seem as if there has been fairly generous provision for the division of general church property of this character.
Then finally the unionists laid a good deal of emphasis on the fact that this union might be in the interests of the country at large, and particularly in the interests of the West. It does not seem to me that it is a question for

United Church of Canada
parliament as to whether or not this union is in the interest of the country. It is our work to deal with this bill.
Those opposed to the union, representing one section of the Presbyterian church, claim through their counsel and through others who spoke for them, that the proposed legislation was beyond the powers of parliament. They emphasized the fact that the bill was concerned with property rights, and that property rights was essentially a provincial matter. Further, they argued that parliament cannot divert the trusts from the original purposes, and many eminent authorities were quoted, including Lord Halsbury, and other law lords. They argued that the assembly had no power to annihilate the church-that word "annihilate" was used again and again-that however wide the recognized powers of the assembly, it had no right to annihilate the church, and here again we had quotations from Lord Overtoun in the Free Church of Scotland case.
Further, they laid great emphasis on the fact that the church must retain its "identity of doctrine." The Westminster Confession is recognized as the subordinate standard of faith in the Presbyterian church, and it was said that no church might deviate from this standard and remain a Presbyterian church.
Finally, the opponents of union made the sentimental appeal, and I use the word in the best sense, that they must not be deprived of the church of their forefathers, the historic church in which they had been brought up.
Then there came from the anti-unionists the amendment which is now incorporated in the bill as it is before us. That amendment would result in a delay of action until the case before the Ontario courts is decided -probably two years, or that time might even be exceeded. I quite admit that when prominent legal authorities differ, it may seem presumptuous for a layman to have anything to say on the matter, and yet on the other hand perhaps it is well that these questions should not be decided entirely by lawyers. There are other than legal questions to be considered, and some of us who have not had legal training, desire to emphasize some other than the strictly legal aspects. I cannot see that it is right that we, as a House of Commons, Should permit our powers to be abrogated and relegate, this whole matter to the courts. Here is a straightforward proposition that is brought before us, a bill to unite three Canadian churches. It is not a matter for the courts to decide whether the bill is in order or not. We are the people who Should decide
that. I admit there are certain legal and technical difficulties, but supposing the courts should decide that this bill was not constitutional; what would happen? The whole matter would be delayed for several years, involving an immense amount of friction, and finally it would undoubtedly come back to parliament again, because parliament would be the only body that could ultimately decide a matter of this kind. This was done in the famous Scottish case where the whole question was referred to parliament, which went behind the merely legal points to secure substantial justice.
Let me comment very briefly on a few points. In the matter of provincial rights I believe the bill is very carefully drawn. An effort has been made in every instance to avoid any trespass on provincial rights as they affect local church property, and moreover concurrent legislation is being sought in all the various provincial Legislatures. I should like to point out in passing that if the bill meets shipwreck on this ground of provincial rights it may possibly result in some good, as it may give the general public a little more sympathy with some of us who have brought forward measures in this House only to be told again and again that we cannot act because of provincial rights. It was only the other day that we had the eight-hour day issue before us, and again it was a question of our not being able to take action because such matters were within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
With regard to the question raised by the chairman of the committee (Mr. McGiverin), and others, on the administration of trusts there appeared very clearly two fundamentally divergent conceptions of what the church really was. On the one side the church was regarded as a fixed organization irrevocably based upon one unalterable standard of doctrine. On the other hand the church was regarded as a living organism, adapting itself to the new conditions in which it finds itself existing. Now, I would ask if all these matters are to be settled on the ground of precedent, as the lawyers generally do settle these things;
*-as their training inclines them to settle them. -How are we to decide which of these two conceptions of the church is to prevail? If we are to regard the church as a fixed organization based upon unalterable doctrine, one decision must be given. If, however, as some of the law lords pointed out in the Scottish case, the church is an organization that may modify its creed and policy from time to time as all other human institutions do, then another decision would perforce be given. On
United, Church of Canada

the general question of trusts why should we allow the dead hand of the past forever to tie action in the present? Because some man one, two or three decades or two or three hundred years ago gave a certain donation in all good faith, and notwithstanding changed conditions must we tie the hands of the people of to-day who are trying to grapple with the problems that meet us from day to day? That is really the argument that is brought forward, and that argument, I believe, a great many of us cannot possibly subscribe to or allow to prevail.
As to the statement that the assembly has no power to annihilate the church I would suggest that this takes the whole question for granted. Surely the church itself is the best judge of what its real life is. I think I may lay that down as a general principle-that the church itself must remain the judge of what its real life is. We are told that if the church unites it loses its name, it loses its identity. Well, let me give an illustration in regard to that. A young woman is married. She loses her name. Does she lose her identity?
I should say not.
Is she annihilated?
No.

Surely in practice we recognize that sometimes there may be a merging of one life into a fuller life. That is the attitude that we take in regard to other matters and surely it is not right to say that because there is a change of relation, the individual or corporation which enters into the new relation is thereby annihilated. The changes have been rung on two terms. I do not pretend to distinguish the exact meanings of these terms-"identity" and "entity".
I submit that these are metaphysical and legal abstractions. So far from the lawyers saving us from the difficulties in the case they are largely responsible for the tangle into which we have got ourselves. Let us view the situation from the practical standpoint. The unionists say that the church must go into the union as an entity, and as the bill was first drafted I confess it seemed to me that the people who would not go in were left suspended between heaven and earth. As there could be but one entity, if the Presbyterian church went into that union the whole church went in, and there was nothing left out. But some of the anti-unionists feel that they are very real personalities and they did not know where they were. I do not blame them for feeling that way as it is a legal interpretation that since the entity had gone into the union there was nothing left outside.

On the other hand the anti-unionists, the non-concurrents, claim that they are the only true Presbyterians and hence the entity is outside the union and the individual people that go in, go in on their own account but that it is not the Presbyterian church that is going in. So we have the one group saying they are "it" and they are going in, and the other group saying they are "it" [DOT] and are staying out.
Now I want to look at this matter not from the legal or theological standpoint but from the standpoint of common sense. The fact is that the Presbyterian church, as far as we on the committee could judge, is irrevocably divided; it is divided into two groups. One group has gone into the union, the other has stayed out of the union. And what is the reason for all this talk of identity? The real reason is because certain property rights lie at the basis of it. If the unionists can establish that they are the true church, they carry the property with them; and if the antiunionists can establish they are the true church, then they retain the property. That is the real reason why there is so much stress laid by the lawyers on this question of identity. Mr. Lafleur, the counsel for the anti-unionists built up the greater part of his legal argument on what he called the doctrinal basis of identity. Every Presbyterian minister is required to answer this question on his ordination or induction:
Do you believe the Westminster Confession of Faith, as adopted by this church in the basis of union, to be founded on and agreeable to the word of God, and in your teaching do you promise faithfully to adhere thereto ?
A similar question is asked of the elders and deacons. The Westminster Confession of Faith, according to the basis of union of the present Presbyterian church, forms the subordinate standard of the church. I am inclined to think that there is something in the charge that the anti-unionists bring in this case because no less an authority than Sir Robert Falconer said that 90 per cent of the ministers in the Presbyterian church subscribed to that basis of faith only with reservations. On the other hand I want to ask whether all the anti-unionists really believe in the Westminster confession? There are very few copies of the Westminster Confession of Faith now available to the public. We have had certain clauses of it read before the committee and in order that the House may know what are some of the things for which the anti-unionists stand and to which they pin their whole legal argument I should

United Church oj Canada
like to read one or two of these clauses. Chapter 3, section 3 reads:
By the decree of God, for the manifestation of His glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others foreordained to everlasting death.
Chapter 6, section 1 reads as follows:
Our first parents being seduced by the subtlety and temptation of Satan, sinned in eating the forbidden fruit. This their sin God was pleased, according to His wise and holy counsel, to permit, having purposed to order it to His own glory.
Chapter 10, section 3 and 4 reads:
III	Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the spirit, who worked when, and where, and how he pleaseth. So also are all the elect persons who are capable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the word.
IV	Others not elected, although they may be called by the ministry of the word, and may have some common operations of the spirit, yet they never truly come unto Christ, and therefore connot be saved; much less can men not professing the Christian religion be saved in any other way whatsoever, be they ever so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the law of that religion they do profess; and to assert and maintain that they may is very pernicious, and to be detested.
Chapter 25, section 6 reads:
There is no other head of the church but the Lord Jesus Christ; nor can the Pope of Rome in any sense be head thereof; but is that antichrist that man of sin and son of perdition that exalteth himself in the church against Christ and all that is called God.
Now it is not for us in this House to say whether that doctrine is correct or not, but my point is that the whole legal argument of the anti-unionists is built upon the idea of the identity of doctrine-a doctrine that cannot be altered-and that the subordinate standard of faith is the Westminster confession, one or two clauses of which I have read, and which every minister must promise not only to believe but to teach. I ask in all fairness whether the men who adopt this position subscribe unreservedly to every word of this creed. If they do-and I can scarcely conceive it-their case from their standpoint, of unalterableness of doctrine is won; but if they cannot subscribe to that without any reservation, I submit that the legal argument on which they have built up their case absolutely falls to the ground.
There are one or two larger issues that are involved which I must mention very briefly. There is the whole relationship of church to state. We as a state claim to be sovereign. The church as a church claims to be sovereign. Now can you reconcile those two sovereignties. I take it that the only possible way of doing so is by remembering that each must be sovereign in its own sphere. I asked a question of the senior member for Ottawa
i Mr. MeGiverin) a little while ago, when he suggested that the courts should decide the questions of doctrine and of faith. Surely no self-respecting church could submit to a decision by the courts. The church must maintain its supremacy in spiritual matters, and it cannot allow itself to be induced to submit its doctrines to a court or even to parliament. On the other hand, there is undoubtedly the danger that we may build up an ecclesiastical organization that may imperil the state itself. There have been whispers going around the corridors-they have not come before the House perhaps to-day that one of the dangers in this proposed merger is that we should establish a body that will be strong enough to dominate or at least to influence the political life of this country.

Might I ask the hon. member
what ecclesiastical organization he refers to?
I refer to the proposed church merger which three strong churches might become powerful enough in this country to influence the political life of this country.

And endanger the national
life?

The question has been discussed as to whether it is wise for parliament to sanction a strong merger of this kind, lest it put a strong church in the field which would have an adverse influence over the policies of the country.

What is my hon. friend's
opinion?

I would say that
such a danger is not quite so fantastic as perhaps my hon. friend might imagine.
I did not deal with it fantastically.

Since my position
has been questioned, I would read in this connection a circular which was sent out several years ago by one of the churches that proposes to enter the union. It was sent out by the Department of Social Service and Evangelism of the Methodist church, and was dated Toronto, December 7, 1917, addressed as follows:
To the Methodist people of Canada. Declaration by the executive committee of the General Board of Social Service and Evangelism.
The present duty and paramount responsibility of Canada is to render every possible assistance made for the very highest sacrifices and unity in the most determined purpose to contribute its full share to
United Church of Canada

win the war, and thus protect the smaller nations against the menace of an aggressive militarism, save democracy from German autocracy and despotism, and establish the dominance of the principles of Christ in international relationships.
And again:
All our annual conferences were imbued with this spirit. Each adopted strong declarations in favour of selected conscription and Union government.
At the polls on December 17, 1917, every Methodist elector, women as well as men, should conscientiously meet personal responsibility and both vote and work for the election of the candidates who stand with the Union government.
And again:
With enthusiastic unanimity, believing the present duty of every Canadian citizen is to support Union government at the forthcoming election, this executive committee of the Board of Social Service and Evangelism of the Methodist church requests that this statement be read from our pulpits and published in the daily and weekly press. We also urge that every Methodist having the right to vote will support the candidates who are supporting the Union government.
I would submit that if a body is to take that attitude of interfering with political matters it might very well be that it might become a danger to the state.
The only possible solution of this question is what has been expressed in the well-known phrase, "A free church in a free state" I believe the church has an absolute right of freedom of self-determination, of deciding whether or not it wants to enter into union with other bodies. I believe that is an inherent right; but on the other hand I urge that we as representing the state have a right to insist that the church must keep its own place and deal with what have been termed spiritual matters, rather than entering upon these definitely political alignments. As we were struggling in committee with these questions of property rights there kept running through my mind the old saying that is attributed to the one who is claimed as the founder of the Christian church:
And one of the company said unto him, Master speak to my hrother, that he divide the inheritance with me.
And he said unto him, man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetouness; for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
I submit that essentially the struggle before parliament to-day is a struggle for certain property rights, for the control of certain very valuable properties in this country. The emphasis on the question of "identity" by these churches is not because of the idea of apostolic succession which is common to the Episcopal churches. The struggle is not one [Mr. Woodsworth.j
for the right to use a particular name, for there is no reason under the sun why the nonunionist Presbyterian cannot go out to-morrow and use the name Presbyterian. The only name that they may not use is the exact name Presbyterian Church in Canada, and that for purely legal reasons, lest there should be some question over property rights. A great deal has been said by both sides each claiming that the struggle is a struggle for religious liberty. I cannot see that this is at all a struggle for religious liberty. Presbyterians who want to remain Presbyterians and to accept holus-bolus the Westminster confession can remain Presbyterians and no one in this country will say them nay. The unionists, if this bill is defeated, can go into union with every provision in this bill except property clauses and no one will say them nay. Let us face that fact. The real situation is that the rival groups are not content with regard to property arrangements.
That brings me to the point which I should like to emphasize before I close. I cannot think that the present bill contains a sufficient safeguard for the minorities. As far as I can judge the division of the general property is as fair as can be arranged. In fact, it is more generous than any provision that has been made in any previous union. But when we come to the property of minorities within congregations, it does not seem to me that the bill is quite fair. That, after all, is the question with which we are concerned in this parliament. I have mentioned doctrine, not because I wish this parliament to discuss doctrine. I have mentioned church organization, not because I believe this is a matter that we are asked to decide. But we are asked to decide the question of a fair division of property between the two sections of the Presbyterian church,-the other two churches apparently being satisfied with the union arrangement. So, my suggestion is-and I should like to offer it, perhaps, as an amendment at a later stage in the bill if no one else does so-that we should, where necessary, go below the congregational unit and endeavour to provide that no minority is penalized by the proposed union. At the present time a congregation may vote itself into union or out of union, but it goes as a congregation. If in any congregation there is, we will say, 40 per cent of a minority, that minority of 40 per cent has no legal claim on the property. That seems to me to be a hardship and none the less so because it works both ways. If the majority is a unionist majority, it is a hardship for the minority that remains Pres-

byterian. On the other hand, if the majority is Presbyterian, it is undoubtedly a hardship for the unionists.
I will give a particular example of this in my own city of Winnipeg. I am given to understand that in that city every Presbyterian congregation is in favour of church union, but in a number of local churches there are very substantial minorities. I am told that a somewhat similar situation prevails in Saskatoon, Regina, Moose Jaw and Edmonton where the vast majority are in favour of union, but where there are substantial minorities. What happens in such a case? It means that people who have worked for years to build up a common cause would be, by this bill, if it becomes law, deprived of all rights in that local church property. They would not have a right as a minority even in the general church property. I am told by the lawyers-and I suppose I must accept their ruling in this regard-that it will be impossible for us in the Dominion House to legislate with regard to local congregational property; that that is a matter for the provinces to decide. If this ruling is correct, we cannot do anything with regard to congregational property, and that will have to be dealt with by subsequent legislation in the various provinces. But these local minorities within congregations have, in my judgment, certain claims upon the general church property, and we might introduce an amendment to this bill which would recognize those claims and make provision so that as little hardship as possible would be worked upon the minorities. I know that this is said to be impracticable; that it would create a good deal of talk and trouble in the various local congregations; that it might maintain dissension for many years; but any dissension that might take place would not be nearly so serious as the sense of injustice which would rankle in the minds of many minorities if this bill is allowed to go through in the form in which it now comes before the committee.
As regards the bill as amended, let me say again that I think, in referring the matter to the courts, we are not by any means settling the problem; we are merely deferring 'what must ultimately be settled by this House, and further we are putting into the hands of lawyers questions that must be settled on other than purely legal grounds. I shall have to vote for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown).

As
a member of the committee, I should like to associate myself with the committee's report that was I think, well explained by the
United Church oj Canada
chairman. I am not a member of any of the churches that are proposing to effect this union, and consequently I have not been affected as much as some others, perhaps, by the explanation of the various doctrinal points that have been raised. I think, in fact, that in that we have rather gone outside of our sphere, if I may be permitted to say so. A very plain question presents itself to me in connection with this matter and it has done so from the first. It is presented shortly and clearly in a circular sent out by those in favour of union after the bill has been amended in committee. In the very first sentence of that you will read that the object of the promoters of union in introducing the measure is that it will prevent litigation.
That may seem to some a very harmless phrase; but to me it conveys a good deal, and I think we should look into it very carefully, because in it I believe we shall find a reason why every man, who understands the principles that are at the very basis of our constitution, would see that he would stand by the report of this committee. We should ask ourselves: What litigation is it that is proposed to be prevented? Have the parties to that litigation a right to enter upon it and is it within the province of this parliament to prevent the exercise of what I have always understood to be the inalienable and inherent right of every subject,-the right to apply to the courts of the land for justice and more than that, to carry his appeal to the Lords Justices of Appeal, to the Privy Council, as we say figuratively, to the very foot of the Throne I think those principles are assailed in the prevention of the receipt of the report of this committee. I think the matter that was taken up was very carefully considered, as was pointed out by the chairman, the hon. member (for West Hastings (Mr. Porter), and the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth), who gave a good resume in part of what took place, and the report that is presented to the House was not obtained without a great deal of earnest consideration. It does not seem to me, therefore, that hon. members who have not followed the matter up should now, without the same opportunity of hearing both sides which members of that committee had, vote for an amendment to the bill which would destroy the bill as it came from the committee.
Now, the three churches that have been applying for union are old historic churches; it is not necessary at this time of night to remind any one that each of these churches has a very creditable place in the history of our race both in the Old Country and
United Church of Canada

in Canada. But it is claimed that these churches have entered into union and that they have done so by means of their own courts and their own organization, and I do not think there is any difference of opinion in that regard in the case of either the Congregational church or the Methodist church. In the case of the Presbyterian church however there is a minority, we will call it a section of the church, which has entered an appeal to the Supreme Court of Ontario, complaining that the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church in entering into union did so ultra vires of the laws and the constitution of that body. What right has this House to take away from that minority the undoubted right of appeal in this case? If the minority consisted of only one individual citizen this House in my opinion would have no right to deprive that person of the right of appeal to the courts of the land for justice. (But the minority consisted of more than one man. I do not know offhand what the membership of the Presbyterian Church in Canada is, but it has not been claimed at any 'time that more than one third of that church has been in favour of union; and consequently the appeal is made on behalf of the remainder of the church which would constitute as I believe a considerable majority of the members. It might possibly be within the legal power of parliament, because we know that parliament is supreme, but certainly it is not within the moral right of this House to prevent that section of the Presbyterian church, a majority as it would seem, from applying to see if they can obtain what they consider justice at the bands of the Supreme Court of Ontario.
This is not a question of the court or of this House deciding upon the creed of these people. The question that the courts have to decide is whether the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church have acted within the constitution of that church; and if points of doctrine come up to be decided upon I think that any man of common sense who has listened to this debate so far will agree with me that the cold minds of trained judges would be far better to consider such points than would a committee of the whole of this Housie. I say this without any disrespect to the members of this House, but because the judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario are men who have been elevated to the bench by reason of their great ability, their fairness and their judicial powers and because they have trained minds and are able to know what is evidence and to make the necessary comparisons in these matters. 
I do not think therefore that we have any right in this House, indeed I think parliament would be exceeding its moral right, and its public sense of duty, if it interfered with that appeal being taken to the courts.
I	do not know that we need go much further than that. It is pointed out in this
circular to which I have alluded,
II	p.m. containing the objections to the
bill as amended and as now before the committee, that parliament is the highest court of all in the land. Well, we know that parliament is above any other body; it was not necessary to learn this from th^ circular in question, because we know that nothing under heaven is above the power of parliament. That was set forth nearly three hundred years ago when it was established that the government of the land under God was in the hands of parliament; and we know that parliament has arranged royal marriages, the union of countries, the succession to the throne and, on one occasion, has even brought the king to the block. So that we cannot very easily put much above [DOT]the power of parliament. We will grant that parliament has all this power. But I maintain that the more power we have the more Carefully and the more considerately should Ve use it. We should not use that power to block the right of any person or any section of persons who wish to appeal for justice to the Courts of the land.
It has always been considered the inalienable right of the British subject to appeal for and to obtain justice at the hands of the courts. And the history of our constitution, the history of the development of our race, show clearly that it was the passion for liberty and the respect for justice going hand in hand that made our people great, so that British justice is the word that is used the world over when people wish to speak of that earthly kind of justice which is regarded as most nearly like *the divine. When you go back in the history of the race long before there was such a thing as printing and before there were schools or education, you will find that there was a kind of belief in justice among the people, the principle being almost a settled faith with them; it will be remembered that in the trials by ordeal and the trials by combat appeal was made to the justice of the cause. I look upon justice as a sacred quality and one which this House should revere; I venture to say we should revere it just as dearly as we do any church whatever or any combination of churches.
But in my opinion we are asked now to violate the principle of justice in not putting

United Church oj Canada
this bill through as it came from the committee. As the. bill came from the committee it does not deny the right of appeal to the courts, which as I say is the inherent and inalienable right of anyone in the land who wishes to avail himself of it and to carry his appeal if necessary to the very foot of the throne. It may be because I have not made a study of theology or of anything of that kind, but I find it difficult to understand how one set of Christian people who read the teachings of Jesus Christ as I read them would want to take a. church or a minority of a Church and force it into union against its will. That in itself, it seems to me, is not a Christian principle, and I do not think there can be any satisfactory and beneficial union of these churches unless that union is made entirely voluntary upon the part of the contracting parties. Indeed, that was the principle set forth in 1911 by the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church. I do not think that any section or part of any church should be forced into union, as those Presbyterians complain who object to the union on the ground that the church of their fathers is being annihilated. These people state that the union has not been properly and legally consummated according to the laws and the constitution of their own church, and they have the right to make the objection they do.
It would be far better in the interests of real religion if time were given for a union, until a feeling of union could be effected and the difficulties overcome. I do not see why there is so much impatience on the part of those in favour of union to have this measure consummated immediately. They have not taken the bill up fairly as it is before us this evening; they have not shown us what is the difference between the original bill and the amended bill, except that the amendment proposed will take away the right of litigation from those who think they are aggrieved by the passage of the bill in its present form.
A parallel was drawn a little while ago between marriage and the union of the churches. It was said that a woman in getting married did not of necessity lose her identity or become annihilated. I do not think she does in every case. But I could not help thinking when I heard the parallel drawn that in some countries marriages are contracted by the parents and guardians of the young people. To carry the parallel through, it would seem to me as if in this case such a contract had been made and that at the last moment it was found that the bride objected. No consideration. however, is being given to her 228
objection; those enthusiasts who believe in union assure her that she is not going to be annihilated, and they proceed to take her by the scruff of the neck, drag her up to the altar and have the union consummated. I am reminded of a case which occurred in British history a number of years ago, when a royal marriage was conducted on something of the same plan. The royal bride was forced into the marriage against her expressed will, and the comment made at the time by the Marquess of Huntly was that he did not dislike the match but he hated the manner of wooing. That is the case with this union bill. I believe every man in that committee was in favour of church union. From what has been stated here it would seem as though some were in favour of union and some were against- were anti-unionists. But that was not the case so far as I observed the work of the committee; all were in favour of union, but all wanted it to be a union that would be fair and just and equitable, one that would not deprive any persons or any groups of persons of what they considered to be their rights.
The Presbyterian church is an old historic church, the history of which has endeared it to more than a usual extent, I believe, to its members. I have seen strong men with tears in their eyes protesting against the destruction of the church of their fathers. What answer could we give to such men if we lightly legislated that church out of existence or allowed it to be legislated out of existence by taking away from them under this bill that right to appeal to the courts which naturally belongs to them?
I shall not further take up the time of the committee at this late hour. I have indicated sufficiently my stand on the bill. Hon. members can see the real reason why no one who values the traditions of the House can support the bill or vote for it, namely, that the legislation prevents litigation, that is to say, prevents or interrupts the right of certain persons to appeal to the courts, something which should be the inherent and inalienable right of every citizen. I therefore wish to support the report of the committee. The basis of our whole constitution, the greatest boast of our land and of our race, has always been our recognition of the principle of justice. If that principle was ever lost sight of we could not continue to carry on the proceedings of this House. The chairman as he presides over the meetings of this committee represents that principle, just as the king as he presides over the country represents it, in poor imitation of that greater justice which is divine. As far as we can we imitate that justice, and we

United Church oj Canada

should not at any time depart from it. We should regard it as the sacred right of any man to obtain justice as far as he can from the courts of the country, and it is because I feel that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lisgar would have the effect of departing from that justice that I shall have to oppose it.

It is always a pleasure to hear the rare diction and the exceptionally pleasing delivery of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond). In this instance, however, I feel that much of his doctrine is wide of the mark and lacks a concrete application to this case. I would say of the hon. member, with all the respect due to any clever and distinguished layman, that had he been a lawyer I do not think he would have made such an ill-conceived application of legal principles as he has to the particular case in point. But for the fact that I was unavoidably absent from the Private Bills committee during the discussion and the vote on the amendments which it is now sought to delete, I think I should have given a silent vote on this occasion. It happened that that was almost the only sitting of that committee which I missed.
I listened with care to the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) when he argued that this was not a proper case for the committee of the whole to review. He said that the committee below have heard the witnesses and on that point he attempted to build up an analogy with the taking of an appeal from a minor court to a supreme court. Where there is any question with regard to the credibility of the witnesses of course the court below has a tremendous advantage, and the court above will seldom interfere in that respect. But this, Mr. Chairman, is by no means a case of that kind. Let us not on an occasion so important as this forget to be practical. The honesty of the witnesses who gave their evidence before the committee below is unquestioned. Having regard to the character of those witnesses, to their demeanour and to the well-nigh sacred nature of the subjects with which they at times dealt, I am sure that nobody at any time thought of raising a question as to their credibility. In that respect, therefore, the committee of the whole is in the same position as the committee below. Then we have to take into account that, in substantial part at least, the committee below was concerned with questions of law and procedure, with questions of fMr. Raymond.]
theological doctrine. Does anybody suggest now that we are not in just as good a position as the committee below to decide these things according to that doctrine, according to that theory, and according to the facts?
When did this House ever hear the evidence given before the committee or have an opporunity of reading it so that they would know what it was?

I concede that the evidence was not printed, although if anybody had really insisted upon it that might have been done. But the doors were wide open to the public, the gallery of spectators was exceptionally large, and a battery of newspaper reporters was present who synopsized the proceedings and wired them out every few hours. So that there was the utmost publicity, and it is merely an academic argument for the hon. gentleman to say that we are not now in as good a position to look into the facts, theories and doctrines, the law and justice of the case, as was the committee below.
Mr. Chairman, I want to make my remarks brief, and to make them revolve rather strictly around the immediate clause under discussion. As to that clause it is significant that we had a statement from the chairman of the Private Bills committee to the effect that counsel were not heard upon it. I will join the preamble with that clause. I will gladly lay at the feet of the chairman of the Private Bills committee my tribute to the spirit of justice which he displayed, to his fair demeanour, to his attempt to be impartial. I was informed by some of the committee-I have already said that I was not there on that precise occasion, although I attended at all hours all the other sittings-that counsel were denied the right to appear before the committee on this particular amendment. As to the reason for that I am not going to inquire. I know that the chairman had conscientious reasons. Whether they were right or wrong-

It is not fair to blame the
chairman. The committee decided that, not the chairman.

If the hon. member would weigh what I have said, he will find that I was careful not to blame the chairman. I heard the explanation of the chairman that that was by arrangement, but I do wish to be practical to-night, and all the way through, and it is a fact that members of that committee, largely laymen, found themselves at that point, and only at that point, without

United Church of Canada
the expert advice and assistance of counsel as to the exact meaning of that amendment. I will not say they misapprehended the clause; I think I could give evidence on that. I will say it is only too easy a matter of inference that they, as laymen, could well have misapprehended that clause, and it was a thousand pities that the able and reputable counsel for the unionists or against them were not heard on that particular amendment, as to which the committee made it very plain they wanted to hear counsel.
The committee decided against hearing counsel.
Members of the committee insisted counsel be heard.
One.

It may have been one
or more. One may have expressed the wish of many. The significant fact is that counsel were not heard as to that amendment, though heard fully on everything else in this bill, and I ask the House to remember that.
Earlier in the history of this bill there were a great many people in the country, and I admit there are substantial numbers yet, who were absolutely opposed to this bill, and for its rejection in toto. I wish to show that those in favour of these amendments and those against them are much nearer together to-night than perhaps they realize. I think it is scarcely necessary for me to say that I believe this dispute and this conflict has been carried on with the best of good faith on all sides. I saw no evidence of anything else in the committee, and I have seen no evidence of anything else in this House. I am going to assume that that common honesty and that common good faith existed and still exist on both sides. There was a time when the opponents of this union throughout the country were opponents whom I might call out-and-outers. There were witnesses before the committee who wanted, not a modification of the bill, not an amended bill, not a compromise on the bill, but an absolute rejection of the bill.
Hear, hear.
That opened an impassable gulf between the one side and the other. The hon. member for Lunenburg says "hear, hear." He himself-
I said it this afternoon.

And lie says it now. There was at one stage that impassable gulf. Now the gulf is pretty nearly bridged, and I say it 228i
in all good faith, because in this report coming from the committee you get no echo of the voice of the man who may call himself an anti-unionist. Why? There are two classes in this discussion now. There are those whom I will call the unionists, and there are the conditional unionists who say, not that they are opposed to this bill, but that they will consent to it on two conditions; if the bill will successfully run the gauntlet of those two conditions they are unionists too. and will vote for the bill, with all its main features and all its incidentals. Now, can people who take that position really in their reflective moments believe that this bill is fraught with great injustice or any great evil? If they did, what should be their attitude? Independently of what the civil courts might say, or a church constitution might say, their attitude would be:	We shall not suffer injustice; we shall not suffer wrong of a substantial kind; we will still be apposed to the bill and opposed to it without any modifica-t;on of our attitude. Now I wish to tell this House and the country that so far as that attitude is concerned it completely disappeared in the Private Bills committee, and it has completely disappeared so far as this House is concerned. The anti-unionists have completely disappeared, and we have now two classes of unionists.
Now what are those two conditions upon which the conditional unionists are willing that the bill pass? I am not going to be told, I shall not believe it if I am told, that when those who support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lunenburg, setting up as a first condition that if this bill will successfully run the gauntlet of the civil courts and it is thereby decided1 that the Presbyterian church proceeded constitutionally, according to the church meaning of that term, say the bill will be all right under that condition, they had any intention of fraud whatsoever. It would be, I contend, a species of deception, a species almost of fraud, if they felt or if their counsel felt certain in the back of his head that the issue would be sure to be determined against the unionist and that it would' be found that the church courts had not proceeded constitutionally. The very conscience of the gambler will recoil from betting on a certainty, and I say these men were not betting on a certainty. They were acting in good faith, and they said: We are willing to submit a fairly divided probability to the civil courts, and if they decide that the highest court of the Presbyterian church has acted constitutionally we will let the bill come into force. I say it was a fairly divided pro-
United Church of Canada

position, because I do not think anybody here is dogmatic or arbitrary enough, I well-nigh said foolish enough, to say there would be any certainty as to the issue of that law suit which would ensue. No man could be sure of it.
Well then, Mr. Chairman, here we have our pure unionists, and our conditional unionists; and our conditional unionists are merely laying down that if it turns out from the pronouncements of the civil courts-I want to emphasize this-that the Presbyterian church in the strictly narrow sense has proceeded constitutionally, they will let the bill go through with all its blessings; and if the conditional unionists really believe that the bill is fraught with any of its alleged evil or injustice they would let it go through with these too, would they? They are willing to help it through if the civil courts will do so. I say that proves that nobody in this House is unalterably or unreasonably opposed to union. It proves that not even the conditional unionists consider that this bill is really a very bad one.
Perhaps I am compelled to withdraw the word " unreasonably," because after all I think our attitude should be to treat this matter largely on its merits, not to make an idol of the constitution of the church to the extent of saying that the technical reading of its constitution shall determine the life or death of this bill, quite independent of the merits or the demerits of the conflict and controversy which have been created around this particular measure. It is true that they ask us to run the risk of another conflict which is this: That if the Supreme Court will say that this parliament has jurisdiction to pass the bill as respects that part thereof which professes to deal with federal legislation, then they will be prepared to allow that part to go into effect and take the results. I say that in this respect it is another place wherein those who support this amendment,-the conditional unionists as I term them for the want of a better name, and I do not say that with any disrespect,-will find themselves under the most grave danger that the union bill would run that little risk. Because-and I think I may say this without incurring any risk of being guilty of bad taste-there is a statement from the Deputy Minister of Justice and there is no sounder lawyer within the bounds of the Dominion. He has given his opinion that there is no question that on this second branch of these two conditions the unionists are in the right and that this parliament has jurisdiction. I do not profess for a moment to be anything more than a very humble lawyer but I will say this-that if 
as between the provincial and the federal jurisdiction we have not the power to unite bodies of this kind it is high time we knew why, and it is high time that our constitution in that respect should be amended. Personally I have the belief that there is ample power, and that if the conditional unionists are counting on only a bare chance on that branch of their amendment they would lose.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice. That is very important. Was that opinion committed to writing, and is it available?

I could not say as to that,. I am very credibly informed that the Deputy Minister of Justice gave that opinion, and 1 asked my informant whether it would be proper to make this statement on the floor of parliament.

The hon. member has stated that the deputy minister has given such an opinion, and I have not the slightest doubt that when he makes the statement he is correct. But I think other members are entitled to the information if it is available. It is certainly very important inasmuch as it involves one of the very amendments to this bill.

I cannot guarantee that
we can get the opinion in writing; I have had no immediate experience in regard to that feort of request. I feel absolutely certain, 'however, that the opinion was unequivocally 'given by the Deputy Minister of Justice.

Will the hon. member tell
tne to whom the information was given?

If I gave the name it
'would carry absolute respect throughout 'Canada, but perhaps the hon. gentlemen will excuse me from linking up any further name in this connection.

I am not trying to pry into
anything of a private nature, but if we can get the information, it will prove advantageous to every member of this House. If this is a private matter I can assure the hon. member I do not wish to press my request, but 1 would have thought, however, that if the Deputy Minister of Justice had been asked for an opinion on this very important matter 'that opinion would have been available to dll the members.

I can only say that when
I have completed my few rambling remarks I shall be very glad to see the hon. member privately and ascertain whether Mr. New-

United Church of Canada
combe's opinion can be again disclosed and whether we can giet it in writing. I do not doubt the good faith or question the courtesy of my hon. friend in pressing his question as he has done. Now then, if we admit that there is at least a fair probability that on the last branch of this amendment the conditional 'unionists would lose and the real unionists "would win, it simply resolves itself into the sole remaining question of whether we are going to make such an idol of the strict technical interpretation of the constitution 'of the Presbyterian church as that it must 'permanently hold back a great movement of this sort, as that it must be considered as something upon which human hands may scarcely be laid at all.
Our friends who support the challenged amendments to this bill lappeal -bo the case 'of the Scottish church in the Old Country. I have no quarrel with that except that those 'gentlemen do not go the full length of the experience there. That is to say they settle tipon the result of the litigation: they will not go to the next step and look at -the re-'suLt, and look at the initiation, of the legislation. It is -true -that the two Presbyterian 'churches which tried to imite in Scotland- the Free church and the United Presbyterian-made a constitutional mistake. It turned upon a very small matter indeed, and as the case ran through the Scottish courts each one of those courts said that no mistake 'had been made; that the churches had -perfect authority to unite as they did without any recourse to parliament. It came up to the House of Lords, because that -body of course is the highest court of appeal in such a matter. They weighed the matter and they were divided -three to three. In that event, but for the death of Lord Shand, the decisions of the Scotch courts would have stood hod it would have been proclaimed -to-day that those churches united properly without any recourse to parliament. When Lord Shand died there was a re-hearing and the majority by four to two decided that be-'cau.se -the Free church departed in & slight 'particular on a. question of what was called patronage from the d-ootrine which i-t had believed in former years, but which even then had lain dormant for many years, it could not carry property with it, and therefore in h practical sense the union could not be con-'summated. What did they do? They immediately went to the Mother of Parliaments herself, and she gave corrective legislation Itpon w-hich -I am not going to dilate tonight. But when this Canadian Presbyterian General Assembly sought -bo bring about
'union they -apprehended this very thing. It 'is in their appendix of law, and -there they 'categorically refer to the unfortunate and technically unconstitutional experience of the Scottish church in getting into that little blunder and they said "We will make that right by making the legislation supersede the possible law suit". In Scotland -the law suit bame first and the corrective legislation- afterWards. Here we are putting -the "legislation first. We cannot prevent anybody from going -to law, but we want to -make -it -humanly 'certain that nobody can disrupt -this union by carrying tedious litigation into our civil courts for a pronouncement.

Would my hon. friend permit me a question on the second clause? He has dealt with -the reference which -the present bill provides -to t-h-e courts on a constitutional question under the British North America Act. Would he agree with me that is a question that those who are opposed to this act can "have tried no matter what this 'parliament does?

That they can -have
tried-is that what my hon. friend is asking?

Suppose we put the bill
through with that clause out, it would be quite proper in the pending suit to have that very question decided in the courts; in other words to ascertain whether or not the act would be ultra vires; and if the act were held to be ultra vires, you would then have the whole union which it was sought to consummate upset; and that is a right which they would have no matter what is done in this House.

I do not understand that
there is any pending litigation now which would settle the question. The pending litigation would settle only at most the present constitution of the Presbyterian church in one or two particulars. Of course I am willing to stand corrected. Does the hon. member say the suit now pending would deal with the wide question of the jurisdiction of parliament to pass the bill?

I have no hesitation in saying that the action which was commenced last January, in which issue has been joined, and which is now pending for trial in Toronto involves the two questions, namely the right of the General Assembly to do what they did, and also the question of property and civil rights. It is alleged that this very act assumes to deal with property and civil rights, and that therefore this act is ultra vires.

United Church oj Canada
If I could feel that there was any doubt about that latter point, I would think it a great pity that the point could not be decided before this measure is further dealt with.

That is the way I feel about
it. That suit will be pressed to a decision in any event, and is it not better to obtain a decision and know where we are, rather than to have union consummated, and then to have the courts decide that union is ultra vires? Such a decision would produce a chaotic condition.

I find myself unable to
take that view very seriously, namely as to whether this federal parliament has the right to go as far as it professes to go in this bill. I now therefore come back to my first position, that I do not think there is anything in the doctrine of the Presbyterian church which would tie the hands of this church forever if it wanted to consummate a union with some other body of worthy Christians. That is the effect of one branch of this amendment: Submit that to the civil courts and see what they think about it. Quite apart from that immediate aspect of the matter, the church is not supposed to run to the civil courts to have those courts pronounce upon its own constitution. In the Old Country it was decided, perhaps narrowly, that the church must do that. In the United States we find that the civil courts would refuse to review the constitution, the discipline, the procedure, or any such cognate matters, of the church as has been done in Britain. The matter simmers down to this:	If you could submit to an
American court the question of the constitutionality, the first branch of the amendment, to the United States courts, they would say, "We will not interfere with what the General Assembly of the church in the United States has done". That matter was decided in a case in the Supreme Court of the United States. I will read a few lines from the judgment in that case to show the view they held as compared with the British view. I refer to the case of Watson versus Jones, Supreme Court of the United States Reports, volume 80, pages 679-789, and I read from the controlling judgment as follows:
We can very well understand how the Lord Chancellor of England, who is, in his office, in a large sense, the head and representative of the Established church, who controls very largely the church patronage, and whose judicial decision may be, and not, unfrequently is, invoked in cases of heresy and ecclesiastical contumacy, should feel, even in dealing with a dissenting church, but little delicacy in grappling with the most abstruse problems of theological controversy, or in construing the instruments which those 
churches have adopted as their rules of government, or inquiring into their customs and usages.
Then the judgment gives the American view as fallows:
It is not to be supposed that the judges of the civil courts (in the United States) can be as competent in the ecclesiastical law and religious faith of all these bodies as the ablest men in each are in reference to their own. It would therefore be an appeal from the more learned tribunal in the law which should decide the case to one which is less so.
We have said that these views are supported by the preponderant weight of authority in this country, and for the reasons which we have given, we do not think the doctrines of the English Chancery court on this subject should have with us the influence which we would cheerfully accord to it on others.
