Now when we consider that the Presbyterian Church in the United States is many times as large and wealthy an organization as the Presbyterian Church in Canada by reason of the population and wealth of that country, and when we consider that that church in the United States is renowned for its generosity and philanthropy, that it will not bow to the civil courts there upon any question of its own constitution, and is not compelled to do so, it is a fair question whether in Canada the Presbyterian church should not follow the rights of the Presbyterian Church in the United States, rather than to go to England for its law in an extremely close decision in that respect. In England the Lord Chancellor is technically head of the church and not afraid to grapple with questions of theology and church constitution.
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) spoke very feelingly about the rights of the minority. He thereby made the confession that those who are not unionists are in the minority, which in a sort of hesitating way has been widely denied by those whose attitude is extreme. Now we have to take into account the rights of the majority as well as the rights of the minority. What chaos would follow, and what an abnormal condition of affairs would ensue, if the majority of the Presbyterians, and the overwhelming majority of those who speak in the Presbyterian church courts, and ostensibly all Canadian Methodists and Con-gregationalists, would find that, after all this preparation they were thrown back where they were before, and that they must therefore in the future lie helpless behind a strict interpretation of the constitutional procedure in the Presbyterian church. There is no question the Presbyterian church has the right to change its procedure. There is a question whether it can change it and carry with it the property.

United Church oj Canada
I was sorry to hear the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) go as far as he did in his contention, because he strongly suggested that this was largely a question of property or a struggle for property. As far as I have watched the motive of both sides in this unfortunate conflict, I think that is furthest from their thoughts. I think their motive is to do more good in the world by the agency of their United church than they have been able to do in the past. I am utterly at a loss to know whether their ambition will be accomplished. I am an adherent of the Presbyterian church myself, although I never felt myself worthy in spirit to enter into the full communion of that church, but from the evidence before me and from the spirit which I see on both sides, I resent the imputation that this is any squabble for property, and I hear men on both sides say that they wish they could divest themselves of the question of property and that they wish they could stand up and convince the onlooking public that they were animated by very much higher motives.
I know that some of the leaders on both sides would be willing to walk out without scrip or purse as regards the church property if thereby they could advance the kingdom which is so dear to them. Whether the unionists may realize their splendid ambition for the results of this union I myself have doubts. I have grave doubts* whether to some extent they shall not be disappointed. But I am asked by the supporters of this amendment to take the responsibility of holding back those people who wish to go forward in this great and spontaneous movement, because the constitution of the Presbyterian church, by a strict interpretation, must be held, as it might be 'held by a civil court, as forever impossible of being changed or departed from. I intend to look at the movement on its merits and to agree incidentally that if the technical church constitution must be over-ridden, it must. It was over-ridden in the Old Country, in Scotland the home of Presbyterianism, and it can be here, without violation of the conscience of any reasonable man. We have been told that there is injustice here. If anybody even at this stage can show wherein that injustice lies and can propose feasible amendments whereby, on the property question or on any other question where injustice is alleged, this bill can remove that injustice, I shall give it my support. But for the meantime-and I came to this decision after a great deal of thought; I have kept an open mind on the subject all through the hearings I have attendedalthough as an adherent I had at an early stage voted against this proposal for union,
I have come to the conclusion that it is my undoubted duty to support the bill with this cardinal amendment removed.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
In the remarks which
I propose to address to the committee at this stage, I wish it to be distinctly understood that I am not speaking for the government of which I am a member. It is well understood that upon this great subject there is a division of opinion amongst the members of the government just as there is amongst members of the party to which we are attached, and amongst the member., of all the parties which are to be found in this House. Personally, my attitude in regard to this matter is that I am opposed to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I wish to point out to the committee the position in which that amendment stands and to raise the point that it should be ruled out of order. If the committee will direct its attention for a moment or two to the matter which I am about to submit to it, I feel sure that hon. members will agree with me in the conclusion at which I have arrived after considerable deliberation. I hesitated about bringing this question to the attention of the committee before I had thoroughly and completely satisfied myself as to the impropriety of the amendment of the hon. member and as to the position which I am taking being absolutely correct. The position of the matter is as follows: Section 2 in this bill is the matter under consideration and the question has been put by the Chairman. The hon. member for Lisgar gave notice that, in regard to section 2, he would move this afternoon as follows:
That the whole of section 2 of the said bill be stricken out.
The committee will notice that the proposition is that the whole of section 2 be stricken out:
And the following substituted therefor:
2.	This act shall come into force on the 10th day of June, 1925, except the provisions required to permit the vote provided for in section 10, being taken, which shall come into force on the 10th day of December, 1924.
3.	And that section 10, subsection "B", be amended by adding thereto the words, "On matters affecting the disposal of property."
My hon. friend proposes first that the section be stricken out, and he proposes this by way of amendment. He also proposes that two distinct substitutions shall be made.
United Church oj Canada
The last part of the. amendment No. 3 is not part of the amendment that I moved this afternoon. That is an amendment that was intended to be brought up when that stage of the bill was reached.

If the hon. member wants to have the section that he has marked here, section 3, considered at a later stage of the bill, he had better give a new notice, because the notice is applicable to two distinct sections. I take it, of course, that my hon. friend moved only that portion of this clause of which he gave notice which is contained in the two proposals, first:
That the whole of section 2 be stricken out.
And second:
And the following be substituted therefor:
"This act shall come into force on the lOtih day of June, 1925."
The question is whether, under the rules of the House, it is possible absolutely to strike out a section in a bill or the whole of the terms of any motion or question that comes before the House for consideration and to substitute some other proposal for it. If we look at the rules in regard to the question, we shall find that in Beauchesne's book, rule 36 on page 93 states:
When a question is under debate, no motion is received unless to amend it.
That is, by changing in some way the proposed resolution or section or question:
To postpone it to a day certain; for the previous question; for reading the Orders of the Day; for proceeding to another order, to adjourn the debate; or for the adjournment of the House.
Other than for those purposes no motion can be made affecting a section or a question. Clause 331 goes on to state:
A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words.
In an existing resolution or section.
(b) By leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
My hon. friend does not do any of those three things. He proposes to destroy the clause altogether and to substitute another clause for it. In other words, he proposes to do two things at once; to strike out wholly section 2 of the bill and, second, to insert a new section in the bill. Under the rules he cannot do this. As to that the authorities are so clear that there can be no question about the matter. First in May at page 258 there is this statement:
The object of an amendment may be to effect such an alteration in a question as will obtain the support of those who, without such alteration, must either vote against it or abstain from voting thereon, or to present 
to the House an alternative proposition either wholly or partially opposed to the original question. This may be effected by moving to omit all the words of the question after the first word, "that", and to substitute in their place other words of a different import.
If my hon. friend had moved that section 2 of the bill should be amended by striking out all the words after the words_________
This act shall not come into force.
-and then substituted the words which he proposes, he would be within the rules, because he would be altering in some way a section in the bill and leaving the origination of that section, so that his substitution would be regular. But my hon. friend was proposing to do two things. This is the position that the House would be in. A resolution to strike out a section in a bill absolutely is a matter to which we might all give adherence. That is one issue. It would remove from the bill a section which provides certain things. But when my hon. friend goes further and moves not only to strike out a section absolutely, but to insert an entirely new and different clause, the House is asked to vote for two-propositions at the same time, one way or the other. It is up to every hon. member to say first whether he is in favour of striking out the clause or not. That is a substantive proposition. He is also compelled by reason of my hon. friend's proposition to consider whether he would vote for the substitution. Now, that is where my hon. friend runs counter to the rules. The point is so clearly stated by Redlich, third volume, page 94, that if the committee will follow me closely they will agree that no language of mine could make the situation more obvious. Redlich says.
It is irregular to move by way of amendment to omit a whole clause and to substitute another. Such a proposal is equivalent to proposing a new clause. The rules insist upon such a substitution being carried out in two stages: the old clause may be struck out first and the new one inserted afterwards. But the insertion of the new clause may only be made after the whole text of the bill has been gone through and all the amendments thereto disposed of.
According to Redlich therefore my hon. friend is clearly out of order. It is positively stated that it is irregular to move by way of amendment to omit the whole of a clause and substitute another, and that is what the hon. gentleman is proposing to do. That rule is observed for a very necessary and obvious reason which I have already given. If the hon. gentleman desired to have clause 2 struck out he should have moved that it be deleted, and given notice of a subsequent motion at any time for the substitution of a new clause. He could not, however, move at one and the same time that the old clause

United Church oj Canada
be struck out and the new one substituted therefor, because the two things cannot be done simultaneously under the rules. Therein my hon. friend has failed. Now, we have had a debate on this matter all afternoon and evening touching the merits of clause 2. How many hon. gentlemen have discussed the new amendment proposed by the hon. member? I do not think I have heard any hon. gentleman who has addressed the committee throughout the debate give any consideration for one moment to the new amendment which, if it were in order, my hon. friend is asking the committee to adopt. The course open to my hon. friend, if the committee is agreeable, is to withdraw the amendment he has moved. If he wishes to attack the existing clause in the bill he must do so by a specific notice of motion for the purpose, but he cannot by any possibility under the authorities I have quoted do the two things at once. As hon. gentlemen are aware, it frequently occurs in this House that an amendment is moved to a motion which is under consideration. What is the nature of such an amendment? It is to the effect, "that all the words after the word That' be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor". That is the proper form in which an amendment should be stated. But if an hon. member moved that a resolution under con-
12	m. sideration should be amended by its being struck out and another resolution substituted in place of it he would be out of order, as would readily be seen. The ordinary practice in these matters is to preserve the integrity of the original motion by asking, in the amending motion, that "all the words after the word 'that' be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor". My hon. friend however does not propose to do that in this instance and he runs counter to the rules; he asks the committee on a distinct issue to wipe out an existing clause in the bill. He can do that of course; but he cannot, as he is attempting to do, ask the committee to adopt a second clause in substitution therefor. The authority I have quoted from Redlich is positive on the point. Let me refer also to Blackmore's Speakers' Decisions wherein the rule is laid down:
A proposition which is of the nature of a substitution rather than an amendment cannot be put unless the question which it seeks to amend be negatived, when it is competent to submit the motion.
My hon. friend's motion is therefore not in order for the reasons I have given and I submit that the chairman should so rule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does any hon. member desire to speak to the point of order? The objection advanced by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) has reference to a notice of motion by way of amendment appearing in the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons of June 17.

May I interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Chairman?
I want to make it clear that the objection I am taking is based not only on the ground of irregularity; my hon. friend is proposing a new clause altogether, which he cannot do.

Do I understand the
minister to advise us that if the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) had left the word "that" in the amendment everything would be all right, but that the fact that he strikes "that" out as well as all the rest renders his motion out of order? In other words, that that "that" makes the difference?
The position I take is supported by the authorities I have already quoted.

Would not the minister consider this a notice of motion of a twofold character? I have my own idea as to what the committee did, and everyone knows that I support the committee. But I should think it a misfortune if we lost all this afternoon and evening's discussion and if the committee were obliged to go all over the subject again perhaps to-morrow or the next day. I have not had the opportunity of considering the authorities but one is impressed by what the minister has quoted and it would seem that the amendment is not in order. But if a notice of motion had been given to strike out the clause as it stands and a further notice were given that a substituted clause would subsequently be moved I take it from the authorities quoted that such a procedure would be in order. I do believe that it is the sense of the committee that we should get on with the bill and have it disposed of, and I would respectfully suggest to the minister that he treat this as a double-barrelled notice and that we now proceed with the only thing which as he says, has been under discussion namely, the striking out of the clause as it now exists. That can be disposed of and we can then take up the second phase of the question and deal with it.

I have not raised the point of order without a sense of the importance of having the debate ex-
United Church of Canada

pedited as much as possible, for I am just as anxious as any other hon. member to facilitate the business of the House. But I considered it my duty to bring to the attention of the committee the irregularity of the hon. member's amendment. Otherwise the rules of the House might be violated and the present procedure might possibly be regarded at some time in the future as constituting a precedent. Personally I have no objection whatever to any course by which the hon. gentleman can bring himself within the rides. As the hon. member has pointed out, if my hon. friend from Lisgar had given notice of motion simply that clause 2 of the bill be struck out he would be in order, and if he desired to propose a new clause later on he could do so. It is a matter for the committee to decide.

I do not rise to take exception to the objection urged by the minister. I said that so far as I could size the situation up from the quotations he had made, he was quite right. But I do make that suggestion, though I realize it could not be adopted without unanimous consent, and as the minister raises the point his consent would perhaps be riecessary above all. If my suggestion is favourably considered we could simply treat this to-night as a notice of motion that we are dealing merely with the striking out of that clause and with nothing else.

It is entirely a question of the consent of the committee.
I he CHAIRMAN: As I have stated, the Votes and Proceedings of the 17th of June contain notice of this amendment. The question arises whether the amendment is therefore in order or whether it is objectionable upon the ground stated by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald). Rule 112 of the House provides that no important amendment may be proposed to any private bill in committee of the Whole House or at the third reading of the bill unless one day s notice of the same has been given. That rule applies only to private bills, and it puts private bills in an altogether different position from that of resolutions or any other matters that come before the House or the committee for discussion. Beauchesne, in his book on parliamentary procedure, cited by the hon. Minister of National Defence, at paragraph 331 states what is also indicated in May and in Bourinot:

A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
The expression "certain words" would in my opinion mean those that are specifically designated or named or identified in such a way that no one could be misled. In May's Parliamentary Practice, at the same page as quoted from by the hon. Minister of National Defence, the reasons and the objects of an amendment are indicated and the manner in which it may be made. Such amendments are usually made by striking out all the words or a number of words after the word "that;" because all resolutions, as hon. members are aware, begin with the word "that." Of course in this particular section of the bill that word cannot be struck out because the section does not begin with "that." Hon. members wild note that the wording of the section is as follows:
This act shall not come into force until the first day of July 1926, and not then-
And certain sub-paragraphs follow. The amendment proposed is that this act shall come into force on the tenth of June 1925

after clause 2 is struck out, if the amendment, carries. The effect of ruling this proposed amendment out of order would be this: The vote taken in the committee would be taken directly on clause 2, which is the section providing for the act coming into force. If that clause was struck out the act would come into force upon receiving the royal assent. The amendment proposes to postpone the coming into effect, not, it is true, until the date mentioned in section 2, but until a different day. If I understand the minister correctly, Redlich does not go so far as to say that such an amendment would be out of order, though he does say it would be irregular. I am strongly inclined to doubt that its being irregular would mean that it would be out of order. Webster states that amendments are made by substituting something else in the place of what is removed. As was suggested by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), the matter really comes down to the point that if the first word of the section was left in, the amendment would be in order. With all due deference to the objection raised by the hon. Minister of National Defence, I cannot think we are bound by what may be interpreted as the English practice and that we are tied down to an objection of so highly technical a character, and I so rule.

United Church oj Canada

I bow to
the ruling of the chairman, though I entertain my own opinion as to whether he is correct in overruling Redlich. I would venture to address a few words to the committee on the general principle of the bill.
I happen to represent more members of the Presbyterian Church in Canada than any other hon. gentleman here.
I doubt that.

My hon.
friend disputes the 'honour with me; we will check up the census figures and see who is right. I make that claim because I represent a very large constituency, three-quarters of whose people are adherents or members of the Presbyterian church. They have given to Canada and to the church in Canada a number of very distinguished men, men who have played a great part in the history of this country. When I hear hon. gentlemen talk about getting away from the hand of the dead past, I wonder whether it is a good thing for Canada that the achievements of the great men who have gone before should be entirely forgotten, and that we should enter upon a period in which materialism should run rampant and in which all that has stood for solidity of institutions and for advancement in Canada shall have disappeared.
We have given to Canada from the Presbyterians of my constituency men like Sir William Dawson, the first president of McGill University; Doctor George M. Grant, of Kingston, Doctor Falconer, president of Toronto University, Rev. Doctor D. M. Gordon, second president of Queen's University. The Presbyterians of my county are opposed to church union. They voted against it by a large majority in 1915, and since that time they have been misrepresented in the assembly of the church by ministers and those who have the right to go to the assembly and who did not carry out the principle that ought to prevail in a democratic church of speaking for the people who are behind them. Out of ten congregations in my constituency, 3,222 people voted against union and 342 for union, a few months ago. That is an indication of the feeling of the people whom I represent, and I am here to speak for them. I therefore ask this committee, I ask this parliament, to hesitate before taking any step by which that church would be absolutely blotted out.
Let me read to the committee a statement which has been sent to me by the distinguished ex-principal of Queen's, Dr. D. M. Gordon; it puts the story reasonably from the standpoint of those who believe in the church, in
its history and in its great achievement. The statement reads:
Dear Mr. Macdonald,
Permit me to draw your attention to some considerations connected with the bill at present before parliament for the incorporation of the United Church of Canada.
For ten years (1905-1915) I was a member of the Union committee of the Presbyterian church and a warm advocate of the movement, believing that, if it could be accomplished with the general consent of the members, it would tend to promote very greatly the spiritual life of our people and the progress of the Kingdom of God in our country.
At the outset it was stipulated that the church would enter into the proposed union only on condition of the practically unanimous consent of the members. In the report of the Union Committee submitted to the General Assembly in 1905 it is stated that, "It was universally recognized that "a union of the churches to be real and lasting must carry the consent of the entire membership" (Assembly Minutes, Appendix, p. 280) and this was adopted unanimously by the assembly. (Aas. Minutes, p. 46).
I can say with the utmost confidence that if we had imagined that the proposed union could be secured only at the cost of the disruption of the Presbyterian church the movement would have ended with the initial proposal of it in our General Assembly.
That is a very important statement.
As negotiations proceeded year after year and the basis of union was gradually drawn up, opposition to it developed in the courts of the church, so that it was determined to submit the matter to the members to ascertain the mind of the whole church concerning it. Accordingly, the assembly remitted it to presbyteries, in 1911. to consult all the congregations of the church.
It has been contended that the constitution and laws of the church did not require the assent of the members, and that the judgment of presbyteries, synods and General Assembly should be a sufficient guide and warrant for procedure in this matter, as in other important movements within the church, these bodies being entitled to represent the entire membership. No organized society, however, makes provision in its constitution and forms of procedure for its own extinction, and, as the church consists not merely of its official courts but of its entire membership, and as it was now proposed to merge the Presbyterian church in an entirely new ecclesiastical organiration, this action in asking for the judgment of all the congregations and members was both wise and essential. Moreover, the pledge given at the outset of the negotiations to consummate union only with "the consent of the entire membership" could not be evaded.
When, in the assembly of 1912, the votes of the members were received and considered, we were greatly surprised to find a substantial minority opposed to the union. Out of a total registered membership of 287.944 only 155,033 voted; and of those voting only 106,755 approved, while 48,278 were opposed. That is, 54 per cent of the total membership voted: 37 per cent of the total membership for union; 17 per cent of the total membership against union. (See Minutes of Assembly for 1912, Appendix, p. 330).
In view of this opposition, the assembly resolved as follows:-"In view of the extent of the minority which is not yet convinced that organic union is the best method of expressing the unity sincerely desired by all. the assembly deems it unwise immediately to proceed to consummate the union, but believes that by
United Church of Canada

further conference and discussion practically unanimous action can be secured within a reasonable time". (Min. of Ass, 1912, p. 45). Meanwhile closer relations might be fostered between the churches and greater cooperation promoted in missionary, educational and social activities.
In 1915 it was again agreed by the General Assembly to consult the members of the church, but when the vote was received and considered by the assembly in 1916, we were surprised to find that the opposition had greatly increased, that while 106.534 members voted in favour of the Union proposals, 69,913 voted against them. (Ass. Min. for 1916, Appendix, p. 279).
Evidently it would have been wise at this stage to halt further proceedings, even although a majority of presbyteries favoured union. Clearly the time was not ripe for the proposed change. The mind of the church was not prepared for it; and organic union under such conditions would tend rather to hinder than to promote spiritual unity.
Instead, however, of calling a halt in the movement, the assembly in 1916 asserted its adherence to union as the policy of the church; ibut later, in 1917, the assembly agreed to suspend further action dn connection with it until a year after the close of the war. It was expected that the experiences of the war, in uniting all citizens more closely for other purposes affecting the national life, might also move the members of all churches to closer unity.
No further action has been taken since 1916 to ascertain the mind of the members of the dhurch regarding union. Within these intervening years many membens have returned from service overseas and thousands of new members have been enrolled, so that we cannot say what are the present proportions of advocates and opponents of union. Whatever weight we may attach to the many arguments that may be urged in favour of union, and whatever may be our personal predictions in regard to it, the outstanding fact is that there is resolute and apparently increasing opposition to it on the part of the membership of the Presbyterian church. The opponents are probably still in the minority, but they are quite determined that the Presbyterian church must be continued in its present organization.
It is evident, therefore, that if church union is consummated according to the bill for incorporation now before parliament, it must result in the very serious disruption of the Presbyterian church.
I will ask the committee to note the significant utterance o-f this father of the church 5n Canada, one of the most honoured and respected men that ever held a high position in the educational and religious life of this 'country, when he says:
It is evident, therefore, that if church union is consummated according to the bill for incorporation now before parliament, it must result in the very serious disruption of the Presbyterian church. And when it is stated, as in the preamble to the bill, that the Presbyterian church is a party to the petition for the act of incorporation, it should be noted that this is very far from being the petition of the entire church. Indeed, according even to the figures of 1916 (which now it is believed fall far short of representing the entire number of opponents) there is a smaller proportion of members in favour of the act of incorporation than would be required for the merging of two banks or other commercial institutions under the Joint Stock Company Act.

Will the minority, who are determined to maintain the existence and activities of the Presbyterian church, be denied the right to preserve the name of the church as hitherto known? This is to them a matter of serious moment. The. advocates of union claim that by the act of incorporation the Presbyterian church is merged in the United church and therefore ceases to exist as a separate organization. The minority claim that they will continue to be the Presbyterian church after the others have entered the new ecclesiastical organization. Of course, the minority could agree to form a Presbyterian church: not even parliament could prevent this, and the advocates of union admit it. And, for that matter, the body so formed would come to be known as the Presbyterian church. But the retention of the name and the claim of the minority to continue the present organization of the Presbyterian church might, if admitted, be held to carry with it the right to all the property of the Presbyterian church.	[DOT]
This has been one of the chief obstacles in preventing any conciliation between the two contending parties. It might, however, be a matter of agreement between the two parties that the minority should still retain the name but that the estate should be divided according to some equitable arrangement. The advocates of union might fitly be requested to make some agreement with the minority so that they would come before parliament with a united petition for the legislation required in the circumstances.
As to the terms and provisions of the act:-It may be noted that parliament is asked to pronounce upon the spiritual functions of the church as well as upon the tenure of property. This, however, is to ignore the proper functions of parliament. The church has the right to live and act as a free self-governing body with supreme jurisdiction in spiritual matters. It is only in connection with the tenure and administration of property that the church is in any way subject to the decisions of parliament or of courts of justice. In the proposed act, however, parliament is asked to ratify and confirm the Basis of Union and to guarantee to the church freedom to deal with her doctrines and teaching as the courts of the church may determine. While it is a grievous mistake for the church thus to ask the sanction of parliament in spiritual matters, it would surely be a mistake on the part of parliament, even at such a request, to take action outside of its own proper jurisdiction.
Parliament has, however, certain rights and jurisdiction in regard to the tenure and administration of property by the church, as by any other body of citizens,	and	much	of the act is	devoted	to the
transfer of the property of the negotiating churches to the United church.
The attempt is made to arrange for the assignment of certain properties to the " non-concurring " congregations. A commission is to be created to deal with all questions that may arise in connection with the division of the properties of the church, and the decisions of this commission are to be absolute and final, subject	to no	kind of review,	civil or	ecclesiastical.	The	effect,	and manifestly	the purpose, ofthis provision is to forestall and prevent any litigation between the contending parties by closing against them all the constituted courts of justice and forcing them to accept the decisions of this irresponsible commission. The appointment of such a commission could be justified only with the entire consent of both parties, otherwise it is grossly unjust. The minority, however,	are	not asked whether they agree	to this
arrangement, although they may, if they choose, be represented on the commission. It is offered to them as the only tvay to have their share of the propertv determined, and they are deprived of the right, which every citizen is supposed to possess, of access to the

United, Church oj Canada
courts of justice. This is compulsory arbitration with a vengeance! Surely 6uch a proposal cannot be sanctioned by the parliament of Canada as parliament stands for the protection, not for the coercion, of minorities.
Believe me.
Yours very faithfully,
Daniel M. Gordon.
I ventured at this late hour to read that letter to the committee because it is the statement of a man who stands apart from all the controversy that has been waged around this question-a venerable man whose long life has been spent in the service of the church and in behalf of the educational institutions of this country. Retaining in their entirety the magnificent faculties with which he was endowed he tells us that he Started out captivated by the idea that it would be a great thing to have union subject, however, as he put it, to the fact that that union in order to be efficacious should be unanimous. He tells the story of his disillusionment and to-day, in the evening of his life, he tells this parliament, after having viewed all that was likely to happen, that to pass this bill would lead to the disruption of the Presbyterian Church in Canada and inflict the evils that he complains of.
Is that picture a true one or is it not? It seems to me that some gentlemen in regard to this measure forget the genius of the people who for centuries have been connected with the Presbyterian church, the men of Scottish extraction who cherish with great devotion all the traditions of their race, and whose devotion to their church is of the very warp and fibre of their being. They forget the women who have had their children baptized within that church, who have been married according to its rites and the many over whose mortal remains its clergy have spoken the last word. They forget the older men and women who to-day stand looking out into the future. There comes to them some gentleman who says to them " All these treasures of which you are so proud are mere figments of the imagination; they amount to nothing. We will have an act passed in parliament whether you like it or not. We will take your religion from you and when you go out into the great unknown you will have nothing to solace you such as you have been accustomed to depend upon in the past."
_ There are hundreds of men and women in the constituency from which I come who are moved by intense feeling in this matter. I am here to speak on their behalf and to urge the House to hesitate before they take away from those people what they regard as the priceless things of life. Are minorities and their rights to be disregarded in this country?
Sir, I have been in parliament for almost twenty years. I have seen occasions when the rights of minorities were menaced, and the men who stood up for those rights are those who uphold the rights of minorities to-day.
I ask every fair-minded man here to realize that the rights of minorities must be religiously preserved in this country if we are going to maintain Canada as a happy and united country and if it is ever to realize the future we anticipate for it.
I do not propose to speak at any great length. One hon. gentleman in the early part of the debate spoke of the amendment under which this matter is referred to the courts as a challenge to the church. I think that was an unfortunate expression to use. A very large body of men connected with the Presbyterian church originated in good faith in the Supreme Court of Ontario an action to have it declared that the proceeding of those who constitute the General Assembly for the time being in coming to parliament and asking that their church should be destroyed was illegal. I understand that the pleadings in that suit have been closed, and the case stands ready for trial. I cannot recall any occasion in my experience in parliament in which parliament undertook to step in and take away from any litigant any right which in good faith he asserted he had. Hon. gentlemen will search the records of parliament in vain to find where this parliament in its long history ever passed legislation destroying the bona fide rights of any party who, in accordance with the laws of the land, has gone into court to seek remedies and justice. Yet that is what would be done if this bill is passed and the amendments that were made by the committee are disregarded.
These amendments are reasonable and fair. I am not going to travel over the ground that has been so well covered by hon. gentlemen who have discussed them from the standpoint of the view which I entertain, but they provide for an early and speedy determination of the issue on matters of right. That was the object of these amendments. It must be conceded that it is not fair to deprive people of rights which they are asserting in the courts. If we are going to have it laid down as a matter of law and practice in this country that people can be deprived of the rights which they are asserting in the courts that will be a very unfortunate thing indeed. It is proposed to strike out from this bill the provision for a speedy termination of the suit which has been entered relative to a very grave constitutional question that exists, as for instance the right of this parliament to interfere with trusts that have been created and which have been operated under the provisions of the laws of the
United Church oj Canada

provincial legislatures dealing with properties and civil rights. Surely it is not an unfair proposal to ask that this question be determined before the rights of individuals are destroyed and before the claims of those who want to remain Presbyterians are fully considered. That is why these amendments are fair and reasonable, and I submit this committee should not strike them out.
Of what use is a union if it is to be a forced one? The happy illustration given so eloquently by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) in regard to the result of coercive unions is so clear that I am sure it was patent to all. Surely nobody in this committee believes that any union which absolutely destroys or takes away the legal rights of those who want to be Presbyterians will be of any value. If they do, then I regret to say they utterly mistake the genius of the men and women who belonged to the Presbyterian church in the past. It cannot be done. If the action contemplated by the unionists is persisted in all that we have heard about the glories of union will vanish into thin air. There will be perpetuated in this country an embittered feeling, an antagonistic attitude between two great religious bodies; whereas if we act upon the lines of sanity and good judgment, enabling those who have legal or constitutional rights to have them determined before they are forced into a position where their identity is gone and all their property becomes merged in the new organization a very different feeling will prevail.
I appeal to the House to seriously consider before it takes a step that would accomplish no good but would produce evil and injurious effects in this country.
I should like to move with the consent of the Prime Minster that the committee report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I see personally no
necessity for this debate taking place on Thursday; but that is not the point. The statement of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) is absolutely correct. Definite assurances were given time and time again that the report of the Banking and Commerce committee would be taken up on that date. It was postponed on numerous occasions and finally Thursday was definitely settled, and an assurance was given to the gentlemen who desired to debate it. I am not particularly interested because I do not care if the debate does not take place. I merely rise to confirm the statements which have been made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With regard to these various representations that have been made, the only object I have is to try to arrive at some agreement that will best suit the general convenience of the House. It is perfectly obvious that if the Acting

Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) gave an assurance

and I have no doubt as to the correctness of the statements by hon. members that he did-that the debate on the Banking and Commerce matter would be fixed for Thursday, he understood that the present debate would be concluded to-day. I have no doubt he did expect it to be concluded. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), who was leading the House at the time, intimated that he expected the debate would conclude in one day. It is very obvious it is going to take a considerably longer time, and I think there are as many hon. members who are interested in getting the church union question out of the way as there are hon. gentlemen who are interested in having the banking and commerce matter decided. As the church union question has come up first, it seems to me that it ought to have the right of way in a matter of this kind.
Motion agreed to.
